title: Nobody
logline: A week of strange hours: a blowout nobody stays for, a speech about thirty thousand, a drive with no destination — and on the one night he’s where he said he’d be, somebody comes to check.

body: The blind lets the first gray into 412 in slats and keeps the rest of it out. Jack has had five hours. The flight into Santa Barbara came in forty minutes late, Theo drove the SL up out of long-term parking with the top up, and at ten past one they carried the Giant Eagle bag up four flights by a handle each, like two men with a stretcher. Theo put COOKIES — DON’T on the top shelf of his closet, behind a shoebox, and went to bed in his coat.

Some things on Theo’s side are new since Thanksgiving. Over his desk, taped at all four corners, two crayon princes: yellow hair, a crown, a red car, and on the second one a coat to the knees in orange and brown. Tucked into the frame of his mirror, folded small enough to hide under a thumb, a twenty.

Theo is up already, at the MacBook in the navy robe, with a gas-station coffee going cold by the trackpad, and he is reading his News Feed aloud. He reads it the way Father Osei reads the intentions at the twelve-ten — unhurried, with a little rest after each one for the people to answer — in a voice of perfect and terrible innocence.
“*Skye Callender,*” Theo reads, “*likes Jack Costigan’s profile picture.*”

Jack’s profile picture is the one Gina took on the porch on Glenwood in August, the week before he and his father drove out: the gray Mooney hoodie, squinting, because she said *one more* eleven times. He lies still under the blanket and studies the ceiling tiles. The ceiling tiles have nothing to offer him.

“*Jack Costigan likes Skye Callender’s photo.*” A sip of the coffee. “*Jack Costigan likes Skye Callender’s* other *photo.*” Another sip. “*Kevin Tran is studying. Do not text. This means you, Doug.*” A pause. “*Doug Pruitt commented: k.*” Theo lets that one go by in respectful silence before the next: “*Skye Callender likes Jack Costigan’s note.*”
Theo stops. He turns the desk chair all the way around on its casters. “You have *notes*?”

He has one. It’s from February, a snow day, Gina standing behind the desk chair at the basement Dell with her arms folded until he got to twenty-five. Theo has already swiveled back, clicked, and tipped the MacBook’s screen toward Jack’s bed so the room can share.

Theo doesn’t look up from the MacBook. “Fast,” he says, and scrolls.

response: Jack gets up. Jeans off the chair, a flannel off the floor, the towel off the hook on the door, and the phone from the hoodie to the jeans without once coming out into the light.
As he pulls the door to behind him he hears Theo read one more, in the same voice: “*Skye Callender likes this.*”

“That was a one-time engagement.” Theo scrolls. The tops of his ears have gone pink, and he goes on scrolling, with great attention, until Jack has taken his towel and gone down the hall.
“You know her?”

Theo doesn’t turn around. “I know eleven hundred people, Costigan. I know a man in Ojai who sells hats for horses. Little straw ones, with holes cut for the ears. He has a waiting list.” He clicks on to the next story in the Feed — a girl from his high school, and her dachshund in a Santa hat — and likes it.

body: Sully’s is a noise before it’s a room. The *Monday Night Football* music is coming out of every set at once — the big screen over the bar, the tube in the corner, the one over the dartboard — and under it forty people are talking at the top of their lungs about a football team most of them couldn’t have found on a map in August. It’s full on a Monday because Lena told the Newman Center, and the Newman Center came: Peter and Kenzie in a booth with a pitcher of root beer, two of the Veritas missionaries, and Joey Abruzzo, who is a Giants fan from Staten Island, in a borrowed Saints cap he keeps taking off to argue with.
Lena has the chair under the brass bell, in black and gold, and her voice is back. Eight days ago it was a gravel road. Tonight it’s all of New Orleans again, and she’s spending it on a referee.

Julian is on the stool beside her in a cardigan, with a pencil behind his ear and a ginger ale. Under the ginger ale there’s a bar napkin with five lines ruled across it in ballpoint, very straight, and some marks sitting on the lines. Every so often he slides it out of the wet ring, looks at it, and puts it back.

Kevin keeps score on a napkin of his own with a golf pencil, two neat columns, and up the margin, in a box, the day’s other news: WEIS — FIRED. TIGER — WD. Laney, in a Pi Lam sweatshirt with her hair up in a clip, gives the screen her pageant wave when the Saints come out of the tunnel — wrist, wrist, elbow, elbow — and then sits down and starts on Lena’s fries.
“Theodore doesn’t do Mondays,” she reports. “He said it like it was a diagnosis.”
“He told me Mondays are a social construct,” Kevin says, without looking up from the napkin. “I told him so is orgo. He said *exactly*.”

Every few plays the bottom of the big screen runs it again, and the booths have been running it all night anyway: Tiger Woods has pulled out of his own tournament, down in Thousand Oaks, on account of his injuries from the car. “His *own* tournament,” Joey says to the whole booth, in the borrowed cap. “You don’t skip your own tournament. That’s skipping your own wedding.”
“His wife took a golf club to the back window of that car, Joey,” Laney says, with a fry. “I’d skip it too.”
“To get him *out*,” Kevin says, without looking up from the napkin. “The police said she was getting him out.”
Laney eats the fry. “That’s one reading.”

Brees gets the ball, and keeps getting it. Every time the Saints score, the owner unties the rope from its cleat and Lena goes up on the rung of her chair and rings the bell until the glasses on the shelf behind the bar start answering it.
On the third touchdown she takes the rope from the owner, turns around on the rung, and holds it down to Julian.

He looks at it, and stands, and takes it, and rings it carefully, the way you’d ring a church bell — three strokes, each one a count behind where the room wants it. Lena laughs at him, at the bell, at the whole bar, and does the WHO DAT for both of them. Jack, across the table, watches the rope go back to its cleat.

When the Patriots get the ball back she points every bit of the voice at their sideline. “Look at him,” she tells Julian. “That man dresses like he’s been asked to leave a bowling alley. That man cut the sleeves off his own sweatshirt on purpose, in front of God and the network.”
Julian looks. “It’s a hoodie.”
“It’s a *cry for help*, cher.” She takes a fry back from Laney without looking. “And don’t start me on the quarterback. He married a supermodel in February and he still looks *surprised* about it.”
Julian writes something on the napkin that isn’t football.

Halftime empties the place toward the bathrooms and fills it back up. Lena leans across the table to him while the band plays. “You’re quiet. You’re never quiet at halftime. You do the Browns’ whole season at halftime like it’s the Stations of the Cross.”
“They lost to the Bengals. Sixteen to seven.”
“And did you do the Stations?”
“In the garage. With my father. He did the fourteenth by himself.”
She laughs at him and turns back for the second half. In the third quarter the game stops being a contest and turns into a parade, and Joey starts a chant nobody else knows the words to.
At two minutes past seven the RAZR goes against his thigh. He opens it under the table, below the edge, and tips the screen down toward his knee.

s03.slug: MONDAY · 8:50 PM · THE HARBOR, THE LAUNCH-RAMP LOT
body: The far side of the harbor is all noise and almost no light. Sea lions on the bait dock, arguing in the dark about who gets the edge. The water slapping at the foot of the launch ramp. And out in the slips, a hundred halyards ticking against a hundred aluminum masts in a wind too small to feel on his face, like a room full of people tapping pencils during a test. Across the black water the Anchor is a row of yellow windows on the wrong side of everything. Gloria couldn’t see this lot with binoculars.

The Saab is parked under the one sodium lamp with the top down at thirty-nine degrees and the heater going full on the floor. Skye is behind the wheel with her bare feet on the pedals and her chin on her hands on top of the wheel, in something somebody else chose for her: black, strapless, built up stiff from the waist like a wedding cake, with a man’s tuxedo jacket over it that isn’t hers either.
“Don’t look at it,” she says. “It’s a dress with opinions. I came straight from a fitting in Burbank. They wanted to see how it moves. It doesn’t.”
She drove up after: two hours and ten minutes, she says, and she has to be back in the chair for a six o’clock call. “A magazine. I’m not telling you which. You’d look it up.”

He has had nearly three hours of her voice in his ear on his father’s porch and nothing of her face since a parking lot six days ago. The voice is the same one, low, with the day worn into the bottom of it. The face is better than he kept it. Before he’s reached the car she leans across and shoves the passenger door open from inside, and he ends up standing in it with one hand on the top of the frame.

body.text: “You wrote me a *paragraph*, Ohio.” Her hand is already up in the collar of the Carhartt, her fingers hooked in the corduroy, and nothing else about her has moved. “I said the jacket. I meant the jacket.”

body: “Where were you? You smell like a bar.”
“Sully’s. The Saints. I left at the two-minute warning.”
She looks at him over the wheel. “You left a football game early. For me. Where you’re from that’s a proposal.”

body.text: She holds out her hand, palm up. “Receipts.” He has them. Somewhere over Indiana on Sunday night, on the back of his boarding-pass stub from Pittsburgh, he made five tallies and started a sixth, and the beverage cart came before he finished it. She tilts the stub to the lamp. “What’s the half?” “Turbulence.” She considers it, folds it once, and puts it away down the front of the dress with opinions, where it apparently lives now.

body: The heater roars at their feet. The halyards tick. He’s still standing in her open door.

choices.text: Get in and kiss her before the door’s shut.
response: He gets in and kisses her with one knee still on the seat and the door swinging wide behind him on its hinge, and she laughs into it, and reaches past him without looking and hauls the door shut by the armrest.
“I missed you,” he says. “A reasonable amount.”
She goes still for a breath, her hands on the wheel, looking at him in the lamp. “Get in,” she says.

choices.text: “You drove two hours for forty minutes.”
response: “You drove two hours for forty minutes.”
“Two hours and ten,” she says. “And you’re wasting them. Get in.”

s03a.slug: MONDAY · 9:05 PM · THE SAAB, THE LAUNCH-RAMP LOT
body: It isn’t slow. Whatever patience she brought to the lot six days ago, she has left it in Burbank. She has him by the Carhartt before he’s settled in the seat, the gearshift is in the way and then it isn’t, and she comes up over the console onto her knees with the dress creaking like a saddle. She tastes of cinnamon, some mint out of a bowl in Burbank, and under that of two hours of road. She kisses him with one eye on the clock on the dash, and then with neither.

His hand goes into her hair and comes back with a sound. It has been set for a camera and sprayed into place, and it crunches. She laughs against his teeth. “Don’t. That’s six hundred dollars of somebody’s afternoon.” He does it anyway, until it gives and comes down around his wrist.

body.text: “You said my name once and you didn’t answer,” she says against his jaw. His own paragraph, back at him in the dark. “Because you forgot how.” Then she says it. “Jack.” This time he answers.

body: The tuxedo jacket goes over the back of her seat. The Carhartt comes off one of his shoulders and stays caught on the other. His hands go where the dress lets them, and the dress lets them almost nowhere: from her ribs to the top of it she is built in, laced and boned, some engineer’s idea of a girl standing still under lights. It’s like holding her through a fence. She feels him find that out and laughs. “I *told* you. It has opinions.” So his palms go flat on the stiff satin at her sides, and above the satin there is her, bare shoulders and the back of her neck, warm, salt and hairspray, and he puts his mouth there instead and she stops laughing. His hands are cold from the walk across the lot, and when they find the back of her neck she gasps and catches them there with her own and holds them, to warm them or to keep them, he can’t tell which.

On the bait dock the sea lions bark in a row like a heckling section. The windshield has fogged at the bottom corners even with the top down, two gray fans climbing the glass from the dash. Her knee is on the parking brake. The parking brake will live.

Somewhere in it she stops long enough to talk, with her forehead on his and both his ears in her hands. “I thought about this for six days. In traffic. In hair. In the middle of a sentence to my mother.” Her breath on his mouth. “I want you to know that’s what this is.”

He is eighteen, and six days of her in his ear have been going straight into him, and his body says so against all that engineering; she feels it, and makes a low sound in her throat that isn’t a bit. Somewhere at the back of him, in the place that keeps time on Saturdays, a sentence starts with *Bless me, Father*, and the sea lions shout it down.
At twenty to eleven a marimba starts up on the dash. The white iPhone lies lit beside the gearshift, playing a cheerful little tune to the harbor.

“That’s my mother,” she says, into his neck. She lifts her head and looks at it. “No, it isn’t. That’s the alarm I set so I’d leave.” She shuts it off with her thumb and stays where she is a moment longer, breathing. “I’m extremely responsible. Don’t tell anyone.”

body.text: “And I’m not the one stopping this time. I want that in writing. My phone is.”

body: She shrugs the tuxedo jacket back on over the dress and looks at herself in the rearview with her hair standing up. “Six o’clock call,” she says. “And this is what they get.”
“You fell asleep on me,” he says. “Saturday.”
“I know. In the middle of your Madonna.” She puts the car in gear. “I dreamed about a bathtub. Standing up in a yard. I woke up at noon and thought I’d made it up.”
“You didn’t.”
“I know. That’s the part I liked.”

She drives him back around the harbor with the heater on their feet and her hair standing up on one side where he ruined it, and she doesn’t take him to the Anacapa lot. She pulls in at the Marine Lab turnout on Ocean Road instead, where the road bends along the bluff and there’s nothing but a chain across a service drive and a sign about the tide pools.
At the turnout she leaves the engine running and turns to him with one knee up on the seat. “What did you tell them? Your friends at the bar.”

body.text: “That my boss called me in.” “Did she?” “No.” “You lied for me,” Skye says. She sounds delighted, and a little sorry about it, and then mostly delighted.
“That I had somewhere to be.” “You did,” she says. “You had here.”
“That I’d seen how it ends.” She looks at him a moment in the dash light. “Have you?” He hasn’t got an answer for that, and she seems to like that too.

body: “Not your lot,” she says. “Somebody’ll see a pink car and want to know.” He gets out. From the driver’s seat: “Friday. Midnight. Bring a jacket.” She looks at the Carhartt. “That jacket. We’re going nowhere.”

The one taillight goes east along Ocean Road toward the freeway and Burbank and a six o’clock call, and he walks back toward Anacapa with cinnamon in his mouth and his collar still half off his shoulder.

At ten past eleven the Odyssey is under the lamp at the end of the row where Kevin always leaves it, and the back glass has been rewritten in white shoe polish: WHO DAT · 11–0, the 11 in a clean composer’s hand.

body.text: His own ten from last Sunday, the one that leaned, has been wiped off to make room.

“Yeah.”
“Who scored last?”
Jack doesn’t know. Theo says, “Hm,” and scrolls.

s04.slug: TUESDAY · 4:55 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: The sun went down behind the Grove ten minutes ago, and the Lagoon outside the Fishbowl glass has kept what was left of it: copper on the near water, slate at the far side. In the corner the television has West Point — a hall full of cadets in gray, row after row, waiting on a President at eight o’clock Eastern. Along the bottom of the screen CNN has had the number since lunch.

Yusuf came over from Cabrillo for it. “The Abrahamic bloc watches together,” he said in the door, and took the end of the couch. Margot has the armchair and a legal pad. Kevin is on the floor with his back to the couch and the orgo text open on his knees. Lena is on the couch with Julian beside her; he walked over from the UCen with a tea for her, honey in it, the tag hanging over the side of the cup on its string. Laney is painting her nails at the table in the back, uninterested on principle. Jack is standing behind the couch in the Carhartt, with an hour and change before the 6:20 bus and a shift at the end of it.
It starts before the President does, with the number.

“Thirty thousand,” Kevin reads off the crawl. Doug Pruitt, passing the glass on his way to the vending machines with a fistful of quarters, stops long enough to look in at the cadets and say, “Whoa,” and goes on.

“Then send thirty thousand,” Jack says. “If you’re going to go, go. You don’t walk off a job half done.” It’s his father’s sentence, from the garage. “Augustine wrote a Roman general a letter about it. *We don’t look for peace so we can make war. We make war so we can have peace.* Be a peacemaker, he says, even while you’re fighting.”

Lena turns around on the couch to look at him over the back of it. “Augustine also says the intention has to be right, and you can’t see a man’s intention on CNN. And Dorothy Day would be standing outside that gate tonight with a sign,” she says, “and she’d be right, and nobody would listen to her, and she’d go back tomorrow and stand there again.”
“And the girls in Kandahar who want to go to school,” Jack says. “Dorothy Day hands them a sign?”
“Dorothy Day hands them *soup*, Costigan, and then she sits down and eats it with them, and that’s more than a Predator drone has ever done for anybody’s daughter.”
“Y’all are going to make me miss the cadets,” Laney says from the back, blowing on a thumbnail. “I came for the cadets.”
Julian has been listening with his whole face. “Would you go?” he asks Jack. It isn’t a dare; he wants to know. “If you think somebody should.”
“If they asked.”
“They’re asking,” says Margot. “That’s what this is.”
She doesn’t look up from the pad. “Thirty thousand nineteen-year-olds,” she says, “from towns like yours, Costigan. So that a man in a good suit can say a date with a straight face.”
“Towns like mine send them either way.”
“Yes,” says Margot. “That’s my point.”

Yusuf has been sitting at the end of the couch with his hands between his knees, watching the cadets. “You left the first time,” he says. He doesn’t look at any of them. “My father watched you leave. If you’re going to come, stay.”

The Fishbowl has nothing to put after that. Margot looks at him. “I don’t have an answer for that,” she says, and puts the cap back on her pen. At the back table Laney’s brush has stopped over her thumbnail. It stays stopped for exactly that one sentence, and goes on.

At a minute past five the President comes out to the lectern, and the room goes quiet on its own. Kevin reaches up behind him for the remote and turns it up two bars. It takes some time to get there — the towers, the eight years, the families — and then it comes, level, with the cadets not moving: “I have determined that it is in our vital national interest to send an additional thirty thousand U.S. troops to Afghanistan.” And the next sentence, right on its heels: “After eighteen months, our troops will begin to come home.”
“That’s a lot of beds somewhere,” Kevin says quietly, from the floor.

Jack thinks of his father in the garage, who would say *good* to the first sentence and nothing at all to the second. Lena has the tea in her lap. Yusuf, at the end of the couch, says one word under his breath that Jack doesn’t know.
On the coffee table, beside Lena’s tea, Yusuf’s phone lights up and starts walking on the wood. FREMONT — HOME.
Yusuf looks at it for one ring, with the President still talking over it. He picks it up and goes out into the hall with it, and the Fishbowl door drifts shut behind him on the President.

s04a.slug: TUESDAY · 5:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, EAST STAIRWELL
body: Jack finds him by his voice. It comes down the east stairwell from the landing between three and four, low and fast, in a language Jack doesn’t have a word of, with the name *Tariq* in it over and over, like a handhold.

Yusuf is at the landing window with the phone at his ear and his other hand flat on the glass, where the window has been pushed out its six inches and the cold is coming in under his palm. He sees Jack come round the turn below. Jack sits down on the stairs a flight under him, back to the wall, where Yusuf can see him and doesn’t have to talk to him. He has his jacket on and a shift in an hour, and he lets the 6:20 go out of his head.

It goes on a long time. Once Yusuf laughs, short, at something his mother says, and puts his forehead against the glass. The window goes from blue to black. Up on four somebody’s door opens on the President and shuts again.
When it’s over Yusuf comes down and sits two stairs above him, the phone held in both hands, and for a while he only sits, and Jack leaves him to it.
“Tariq,” he says. “An IED. Helmand. He’s alive.”
“Where is he?”

“They flew him to Germany. Landstuhl.” He says it carefully, a word he learned an hour ago. “My mother says they’ll fly him home.” He turns the phone over. “My father’s still at work. NUMMI doesn’t stop for my brother.”
He looks at the dark window. “He had a ticket for Christmas. He sent my mother a picture of the ticket. She has it on the refrigerator.” The short laugh again. “Well. He’s coming home for Christmas.”

journal.title: Yusuf (PHIL 9H)
journal.text: Fremont. Engineer. Fasting for Ramadan through a ninety-minute seminar and funnier than all of us. Broke the fast with his people on Mission Street and fed me till I couldn’t stand. Father on the NUMMI line since ’85. Brother Tariq interprets for the Army in Helmand and calls on Sundays. The day of Fort Hood I asked if Tariq was okay. He’s not in Texas. Friday morning he called: he’s fine, and he said don’t watch the news. Yusuf watched the news. At Hale’s table a man asked him what Muslims think. He’d like one week where nobody asks. His nineteenth, at Bastille, with a candle in a scone. He watched the memorial Tuesday. Standing up. I didn’t ask. The night of the West Point speech: ‘You left the first time. My father watched you leave. If you’re going to come, stay.’ His brother Tariq — an IED in Helmand. Alive. Germany. I went after him. We sat on the east stairs.

response: “Can I pray with you?”
Yusuf looks at him. “Pray however you pray,” he says. “I’m going to.”

So they do it side by side on the east stairs, two ways at once: Yusuf with his palms turned up on his knees and his lips moving, Jack with his elbows on his knees and a Hail Mary going, and then another, for a man in a bed in Germany he has never met. Above them the landing window has gone all the way dark.

Feet on the flight below: Lena, with Yusuf’s gray fleece over her arm, the one he left on the couch. She doesn’t come up. She holds it up over the rail, and Jack reaches down and takes it and passes it up, and Yusuf puts it on. “Kevin’s taking you to the airport at six,” Lena tells him. “First flight north. He already looked it up.”
Jack makes the 6:20 with a minute in hand and rides it into town with his head against the cold window.
Jack sits. Yusuf sits. The stairwell light hums. Somebody comes up past them with a laundry basket on her hip and says *sorry* for no reason and keeps going.
Eventually Yusuf says, “Did you know a Catholic potluck has never run out of food?” — because he has to say something — and Jack laughs, because he has to.

s04b.slug: TUESDAY · 5:20 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: Lena is up off the couch before the door has finished closing, with Yusuf’s gray fleece off the arm of it. Julian half-rises to come with her. She puts a hand on his shoulder going past, and he sits back down.

On the screen the President goes on. Margot gets up, takes the remote from Kevin without asking anybody, and turns the sound down until the cadets are only gray. At the back table Laney caps the bottle and sits with her wet nails spread out on the wood in front of her. Julian holds Lena’s tea in both hands, keeping it warm for her, and looks at the door. “Should somebody —”
“Somebody did,” says Kevin.

Jack stands behind the couch in his jacket and watches a man talk about the rest of the war with no sound coming out. Laney comes up from the back table and sits on the arm of the couch where Lena was, holding her wet nails up in front of her, and has nothing to say about anything. Out on the Lagoon the last of the copper goes.

Lena comes back at twenty to six without the fleece. She sits down by Julian and takes the tea back from him, and Julian moves his knee over against hers and leaves it there. Margot turns the sound back up, one bar.

“His brother,” she says, to all of them. “An IED. He’s alive. They flew him to Germany.” She turns the cup a little in her hands. “His daddy’s still at work. He said the plant doesn’t stop for his brother.”
Kevin shuts the orgo book on his finger.

Lena catches him at the Fishbowl door. “He didn’t want anybody at first,” she says. “So I sat on the stairs a flight down till he did.” She tucks her hair back. “Kevin’s taking him to the airport at six in the morning. First flight north.” She tips her head at the phone in his hand. “Text him something, Jack.”

s05.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:05 AM · THE WHARF, THE RAIL PAST THE BAIT SHACK
body: The full moon is straight overhead, and the wharf planks are white under it, every nail head lit, his own shadow a short black puddle around his boots. He’s off at one. His fingertips are still pruned from six hours of the Hobart, ridged like walnut meat, and the cold gets into them.
The RAZR rings before he’s past the Wharf Rat. The outer screen says SKYE (MISFIT), and under it, *calling*. He answers it walking.
“I’m not falling asleep on you this time,” she says. “I had a Diet Coke. I had two. I can hear my own hair.”

She’s on her mother’s balcony in Studio City, she tells him, wrapped in a comforter, with a five a.m. call; she can’t sleep the night before a call and never could, not since she was eleven, and she wanted — she stops. “I wanted your voice. I’m not going to dress it up.” Behind her, inside the apartment, the parrot says its word once to the dark.

He goes out past the bait shack to the rail at the end, where the Anchor’s windows don’t reach, and leans on it. Below him the harbor has the moon in it. Out in the slips the masts are ticking, the same small racket as Monday, from this side now.
“What’s the magazine?”
“I told you. You’d look it up.”
“I don’t have the internet.”
“You have *Gina*. Gina would have it framed by lunch.”

From her mother’s balcony, she tells him, she can see a piece of the 101 between two apartment buildings, red going one way and white going the other, even now. “It goes all the way to you,” she says. “I checked. It’s the same road.”
“I watched your President today,” she says.
“He’s your President too.”

“I watched him with the sound off. In the trailer. They had CNN on the little TV over the mirror with the captions on, and the captions run about two seconds behind his mouth. So you get the face first.” Something rustles; she’s pulling the comforter up. “He didn’t want to say the number. You could see him get to it. And then he said the date to leave in the same breath, like he was paying for the first thing with the other hand. That’s a man who’s already sorry.”

Jack has the speech in his head as it came out of the Fishbowl TV, with the cadets in gray. He gives it to her anyway. You don’t tell the other side what day you’re leaving; you’ve just told them how long to wait. Augustine says the peace you fight for is the tranquillity of order, and you don’t get order on a timetable. His father would say you don’t walk off the line with the car half built. Somewhere in the middle of it he thinks of his father in the recliner on Glenwood Avenue at eight o’clock Eastern with the *Vindicator* on his knee, watching the same face with the sound up, saying nothing at all. He goes on longer than he means to, on a wharf, at one in the morning, to a girl on a balcony.
She lets him finish. She doesn’t argue the policy at all.

“I don’t know anything about Afghanistan, Jack. I know about faces.” A car goes by below her window in Studio City; he hears it pass. “You want him to be *sure*.” The halyards tick. “You want somebody to be sure.”
“Do the room,” she says. “Who was watching with you. One sentence each, and I’ll tell you who they are.”

So he does the Fishbowl for her, one sentence a person, leaning on the rail. The girl with the legal pad who said *thirty thousand nineteen-year-olds* and then had nothing at all to say to one sentence from the end of the couch. “She’s scared of the thing she can’t argue with,” Skye says. “She’ll be the last one up tonight.” The pre-med on the floor who reached up behind him and turned it up two bars without asking anybody. “He’s the one who drives people to airports.” Jack stops on the rail. “He is. He’s driving somebody at six.” “Obviously,” she says. “Next.” The girl painting her nails at the back, who said she came for the cadets. “She stopped painting when it mattered,” Skye says. “Didn’t she.” She did.
“You skipped one,” Skye says.
“Did I?”
“You did the whole couch and left a hole in the middle of it.” The halyards tick. She doesn’t ask him to fill it, and she doesn’t wait for him to.
He doesn’t have anything for that. So he tells her about the phone on the coffee table.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair.

body: Noon comes through the blue glass and falls in panes across the floor under the ribs of the overturned hull, and Father Osei stands in the middle of it in white, for Francis Xavier.

By the ambo the Advent wreath has its first violet candle going. Kevin is in the fourth pew on the right, with a Bible on the end of it holding the seat. He moves the Bible when Jack genuflects. “Third day,” he whispers. “The Bible was lonely.”
Across the aisle Becca kneels beside Joey Abruzzo, her braid down the back of her barn jacket.

Osei gives the saint one sentence before the Collect, and then a second. “Francis Xavier died on an island within sight of China, waiting for a boat that didn’t come.” He looks out at the twenty of them in the blue. “Most of us die within sight of what we came for. He went anyway.” Then back to the missal, and the twelve-ten carries on as it does every weekday: the twenty of them, the blue light, Mrs. Fitch at the end of the back pew with her purse on her knees and her lips moving a half-second ahead of everybody’s.
At the intentions Jack puts Tariq in, under his breath, and Yusuf’s mother, and Yusuf on his plane. Going up the step to the altar Osei favors the bad leg a little.
After the dismissal Kevin slides the Bible back into its rack. “Tomorrow’s First Friday,” he says. “The Bible has expectations.” He goes off to orgo at a jog.

journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. December 3rd, Xavier’s day, on the steps after the twelve-ten: asked if her saint got there. Pocketbook — where the important ones go. I’m still on the Christmas card list. Daisy’s in the picture.

body: He gets his ten at nine and takes it on the back step, between the walk-in’s compressor and the grease barrel, with the kitchen’s yellow light coming out through the screen door behind him and the harbor in front of him doing nothing in the dark. His hands are pruned to the wrist. At 8:59 exactly the RAZR goes off in the apron pocket, and it isn’t the buzz. It’s the ring.
“It’s nine,” Skye says. “Where you are. It’s on.”

body: She’s in her car, she tells him, in the parking garage under her mother’s building, three levels down with the engine off and the seat back, because it’s the only place in Studio City where you can’t hear a television. Upstairs her mother is watching it with a legal pad. “She takes notes. On *me*. I get them in the morning with the coffee.”

body: “Tell me something that isn’t a lunch.”

So he gives her Hollis 108, half underground, ankles going by the windows; Abraham going up the mountain with the knife and the fire and the boy, and saying nothing to Sarah, nothing to the servants, nothing to Isaac; and the note in small square pencil under his own paragraph. *You answered for Abraham. Who answers for Isaac?*

Skye doesn’t say anything for a time. Out on the water a boat comes in late with its running lights, red and green, and its wake goes slapping along under the Anchor’s pilings long after the boat has gone.

“Nobody asks Isaac,” she says. “That’s who.” Her voice has gone the way it goes when she reads. “He carries the wood. Up the hill. Himself. And he asks the only good question in the whole story — *here’s the fire and the wood, but where’s the lamb?* — and his father says *God will provide*.” A breath, three floors under Studio City. “That’s what you say to a kid on a set. *It’s going to be great, honey.* You say it while you’re tying them to something.”

Jack has the answer he gave Evan, and the one the Church gives, and he gives her both. Isaac wasn’t a kid. Some of the rabbis say he was thirty-seven, and Abraham past a hundred: a grown man carrying a load of wood up a mountain isn’t tied to anything he can’t walk away from. He went up knowing. The Fathers saw Christ in him for it — the wood on his back, the hill, the son who goes up willing. The ram in the thicket. The knife that doesn’t come down.
“That’s a very Catholic way of saying he was a good sport,” Skye says.
“It’s a very Catholic way of saying he was willing.”

“Willing.” She tries the word in the dark of the garage. “Thirty-seven, and still carrying his father’s wood up a hill because his father said so.” A small laugh, not the bit kind. “No, I believe that part. That’s the most believable thing in the whole Bible.”

And then she’s back, bright, all at once, the way a set comes back after a reset. “I’d play him. Isaac. Nobody ever casts Isaac. One line, and then three days of reaction on the way up the mountain. That’s the kind of part that wins things.” She sounds very pleased with it. He doesn’t entirely believe her, and he lets her keep it.
Behind him, through the screen, Rudy’s radio goes to a commercial and the Hobart finishes its cycle with the long hiss it does at the end.
“Your teacher’s question,” Skye says. “The one under the one in pencil. Can you keep a thing from people you love, for their own good?” The garage is quiet on her end. “So. Do you?”

Three levels down, the line holds open a long time. “For whose good?” she says. “Theirs or yours?” “I haven’t worked that out.” “Me neither,” she says, and he can’t tell which part she means. “Don’t work it out tonight.”

At ten past ten, with his arms in the sink to the elbow, the apron goes against his hip, and again, and keeps going. He reads them at the drainboard with his back to the pass.

body: The Fishbowl has gone orange. Theo has put orange party bulbs in both lamps, and the glass walls give the room back to itself over the black water of the Lagoon. Between viewings his MacBook, cabled into the TV in the corner, plays “TiK ToK” at a volume Priya has twice called a choice.
On the door at eye level hangs a placard, laminated, in Comic Sans: THE SITUATION ROOM. Priya came down at ten to see about the noise, read it, and asked the room, “Who laminated this.”
“A citizen,” said Theo, and she left with a fistful of Cheetos and her mouth set.

The Cheetos are in a cut-glass punch bowl with a ladle. Beside the bowl, on the coffee table, stands a bottle of spray tan, unopened, which Theo has declined to explain. *Jersey Shore* premiered last night, and Theo has it again tonight through the cable — eight strangers moving into a house in Seaside Heights and introducing themselves to the camera by their nicknames, and one of them by his stomach muscles — and he hates it with a devotion Jack finds frightening. “Picture it,” he told them at ten, on his feet in a cashmere V-neck with nothing under it. “Eight people. One house. No adult supervision. It’s *Amarcord* with a tanning bed. It is the end of the republic, and I’m going to watch every minute of it.”

Laney dances on the arm of the couch in a Pi Lam tank top whenever the music comes up and sits on it when the show comes back, to boo. She boos every one of them as they come through the front door with their luggage, like the other team’s band. When the little one with the hair arrives with her suitcase and announces herself to the house, Laney points the remote at her like a scepter. “Y’all. That’s *me*. That’s me without a sponsor.” She boos her anyway. Margot has the armchair; she has told them twice she’s here for anthropology. “It’s a kinship structure,” she says, of the man with the stomach muscles explaining what he calls himself. “Lévi-Strauss with hair gel.” Kevin has orgo flashcards on his knee that he hasn’t turned over since the hot tub. “I want that man’s bloodwork,” he says. Doug Pruitt, in his Tauren-druid hoodie, says “Duuuude” at the stomach muscles with every one of its vowels.

Lena is on the couch with her boots off and her feet tucked under her and her head on Julian’s shoulder. Julian watches the show the way he watches everything, carefully, in case it turns out to be in a key. Theo served him his Cheetos last, in a paper cup, and called him Mr. Park-Ellis both times. When a girl on the screen cries on a boardwalk in the dark, Lena says without lifting her head, “Somebody’s mama in New Jersey is lighting a candle right now,” and Julian laughs, low, and Jack looks back at the TV.

Before he runs the premiere again from the top, Theo plays them the voicemail. It has been on every channel since Wednesday, and he has it off a magazine’s website on the MacBook, through the cable, at a volume Priya would call a choice: a man’s voice, low and hurried, left on somebody’s phone. *Hey, it’s, um — it’s Tiger.* The Fishbowl screams. *Can you please take your name off your phone? My wife went through my phone.* Laney falls off the arm of the couch on purpose. Doug says “Duuuude” with a new vowel in it.

“He said *transgressions*,” Kevin says, from behind the flashcards. “On his website. That’s a confession word. You can’t put a confession word on a website.” “You can now,” Margot says, writing. “It’s a genre.” On the couch Julian has listened to the man’s voice with his head on one side. “He sounds tired,” he says, and nobody has a joke for that.

Theo plays it again — not all of it. He drags the little bar back to the middle and lets it say one sentence to the room, *take your name off your phone*, and while it says it he looks at nobody at all. He looks at the punch bowl. Then he puts the show back on.
At 11:52 the RAZR goes against his thigh. He reads it with the screen turned in to his chest.

s10.slug: SATURDAY · 12:05 AM · THE SAAB, OCEAN ROAD → THE COAST HIGHWAY NORTH
body: At five past midnight there’s dew on the chain across the Marine Lab service drive, and the cold has gotten into the knuckles of his hands before it’s gotten anywhere else. The Saab is idling in the turnout with the top down anyway and the heater blasting the floor. She’s in a man’s flannel, red and black, and a gray knit cap pulled down to her eyebrows, and nothing on her feet.
“Jacket?”
He holds open the Carhartt.
“Good,” Skye says. “We’re going nowhere.”

He gets in. The heater is roaring at his boots and the air above his knees is December, and she watches him find that out with real satisfaction. She has a thermos wedged by the handbrake that turns out to be hot chocolate from a packet, and she makes him drink first, and won’t say where she’s been since Wednesday except *places with call sheets*.

She takes the old coast road north along the bluffs, past the dark mouth of the Ellery turnoff without slowing. “Not tonight,” she says, when he looks. “Tonight’s nowhere.” Then the on-ramp, and the highway, and the long climb where the ocean drops away on the left and the hills on the right go black and big. She drives slow for her, in the right lane with the trucks, one hand on the wheel and the other out in the cold.
At the first pothole on the grade the tape deck makes a noise like a sneeze and spits *Rumours* into her lap. Four months of the same side of the same album, and it lets go all at once.

“*Finally*,” Skye says. She holds the cassette up to the dash lights. “I’ve been in a relationship with that tape since August.” She throws it over her shoulder into the back seat like a bouquet and turns on the radio.

It’s a classic-rock station out of Santa Barbara, fraying at the edges, and the first thing on it is a harmonica and a piano, and Jack knows it by the second bar. “Thunder Road.” He knows every word. So, it turns out, does she. She sings it louder than he does and much worse, with her cap pulled down and her free hand conducting the hills, and he sings it anyway, on a highway in California at the top of his lungs with a girl who is on television, and the clock on the dash turns over to one. When the long last part comes she misses the high note by a mile and holds it anyway, past where the song does, into the dark over the passenger seat, and when the saxophone takes it out she lets go of the wheel for one terrible second to applaud.

There are a lot of trucks on the grade at one in the morning, and she gives every one she passes a whole life in three sentences, done before she’s by the cab. A Sysco truck: “Duane. Married twenty-two years to a woman who thinks he’s in Fresno. He is in Fresno, spiritually.” A moving van: “Somebody’s divorce. The good couch. She let him have it so she could say she let him have it.”

s10a.slug: SATURDAY · 1:35 AM · A RANCH ROAD, WEST OF THE HIGHWAY
body: The headlights find a ranch road a lane and a half wide, with no line down the middle and dry grass right to the edges of the asphalt, and a quarter mile in they find the cattle. A dozen of them, black, lying across the road with their legs folded under them and their chins down on the blacktop, and as the Saab comes up on them their eyes come up green in the lights, pair after pair, and their breath goes up white into the beams. Not one head lifts any higher than it has to.

Skye stops short, a car length off the nearest one, and looks at the horn. “I’m not honking at a cow at half past one in the morning,” she says. “I have *some* class.” She puts the hazards on instead — orange on black hides, and off, and on — and leaves the engine running and her door hanging open and gets out barefoot.

Jack gets out his side into the cold, which is worse out here than on the highway: there’s salt in it, and nothing out here but a few miles of grass and then the sea. Skye is crouched in the headlights with one hand down on the road, her cap pulled to her eyebrows, and she looks up at him from under it like she’s found money. “Jack. It’s *warm*.”

It is, nearly. The asphalt has kept some of the afternoon after the air gave it up, and through the knee of his jeans it’s the only thing for miles that isn’t forty degrees. “They’re not stupid,” Skye says, of the cattle. “They found the one heated floor in the county.”

She lies down on it. On her back, in the middle of the road, in the headlights, in the flannel and the cap, with her bare feet toward the bumper and her hair spread out on the blacktop, ten feet from a heifer with a yellow tag in her ear that says 61, who turns her head to Skye with total calm and chews. Skye pats the road beside her.
“Lie down, Jack.”

He does. Grit under his skull, and the warmth coming up through the Carhartt in a slow square between his shoulder blades. The moon is high in the south, three nights past full and lopsided, bright enough to put a shadow under every animal on the road; inland, away from it, the stars are packed down to the black ridgeline of the hills. A dozen cattle breathing, big and slow, near enough to hear each one. Through the open door the radio keeps up a murmur too low to have words in it, and the hazards put orange on the hides and on the side of her face, and take it off, and put it back. He is lying down in the middle of a road in California at half past one in the morning because a girl told him to, and somewhere in Youngstown his grandmother is asleep in her chair with no idea, and it’s better for everybody that she is.
“Whose road is this?”
“Some rancher’s. He’s asleep.” She turns her face to him on the blacktop. “Save your questions. You’re going to need them.”

Skye lifts a fist over her face for a microphone and lets it go at the sky. “Ladieeees and gentlemen. In the black corner.” The heifer chews. “And in the black corner. And in the *other* black corner —” She gives up on the corners. “Tonight’s main event, scheduled for as long as I feel like it: *Questions Only*.”

“Rules. You talk in questions. Only questions. Make a statement, you’re out. Hesitate, you’re out. Ask the same thing twice and you’re out and the heifer gets your car.” The fist comes down onto her stomach, and she says the rest to him, quick, out of the bit. “It’s a real game. We play it at table reads at four in the morning when the script’s bad and the girl across the table wants your job. I haven’t lost since I was twelve.” The fist goes back up. “*Ding.*”
“Why do they like the road?”
“Wouldn’t you?”
“Are you calling me a cow?”
“Are you asking me to?”
“Do you know what I do to boys who call me a cow?”
“Does she?” He tips his head at the heifer.
“Why would you drag her into this?”
“Wasn’t she here first?”
Skye snorts at the moon and comes right back.
“Why is it lopsided?”
“Isn’t everybody, by Saturday?”
“Do you even know any of the stars?”
“Do you want the one with the belt, or the one that’s a dog?”
“Is it a good dog?”
“Is there another kind?”

She means to get him on the stars, and she doesn’t get him on the stars. He’s good at this. He grew up answering *Who made you?* before he could tie his shoes and has spent a semester inside the *Summa*, where every article opens on *It would seem that*, and the questions come off him without any windup at all. Up the road a cow lets out a long sigh through her nose, and Skye points at it without taking her eyes off him — pointing is allowed.
“Who named them?”
“Who names anything?”

They go on like that, quick, up over the stars and back, her questions bright and crooked and his coming level, with the cattle breathing in the gaps. Twice she tries a table-read trick on him — a question so long he might lose the front of it, a question in a whisper so he’ll whisper a yes — and twice he’s asking his before she’s finished hers.
She asks the next one fast and pleased, the way you play a card you’ve been holding since the deal.
“Who made the cows?”
“Who made you ask?”
“Isn’t that cheating?”
“Is it cheating if it’s true?”
“Who decides what’s true?”
“Who decides who decides?”
Skye rolls her head on the asphalt and looks at him. The grin is still there, but she has stopped playing to the cows. Her bare heel has been keeping time on the road, and it stops.
“Are you going to do that all night?”
“Would you like me to stop?”
“Is there a first one, then? A first decider?”
“Wouldn’t there have to be?”
“Does it just go back forever?”
“Can you hang a chain from nothing?”
“Who said it was a chain?”
“What else would you call it?”
She takes a breath of the cold and goes for the throat.
“Then who made the one who made it?”
It’s the question under all the others, the one with no question for an answer, and her face in the headlights says she’s been saving it all drive. The heifer has stopped chewing. It’s his move.

response: “Isn’t it your turn?”
“It is *not* my —” Skye says, and hears it, and it’s too late. She lies there on the warm road and laughs at the sky with both hands over her face. “You’re *good* at this.”
“Is that a statement?”

She takes the loss like a professional, which is to say badly. She wants a ruling from the heifer. She says the dog was a stall. She says that at a real table read they don’t let in anybody who learned the catechism, and he asks her if that was another statement, and she kicks his ankle with a cold bare foot and calls for a rematch in a form he points out is not a question.

The heifer gets up first, hind end and then front, with a grunt, and then the rest of them, by ones and twos, and they walk off the asphalt into the dark grass, finished with the two of them. Skye sits up with grit in her hair.
“Did they leave because I lost?”
“Was that a question?”

In the Saab she kills the hazards and takes the last of the ranch road slow and barefoot, toward the place where the land runs out, and the warm square the road left on his back lasts him most of the way.

s11.slug: SATURDAY · 1:50 AM · A TURNOUT WHERE THE COAST TURNS THE CORNER
body: The ranch road gives out in a dirt turnout on the lip of a bluff, a cattle guard rattling behind them and nothing ahead but the drop and the Pacific. The moon is three nights past full and high in the south, and it lays a road across the water straight to the foot of the bluff, white and broken, so bright the dark on either side of it looks deliberate. Below, a beach without a footprint on it. Down the coast, where the land turns its corner and goes east, there’s a lighthouse that works: a light that comes around, and goes, and comes around.

She turns the engine off, and the quiet comes in from all sides at once: no surf this high up, only the wind in the dry grass along the bluff and, far below, the sea working at the beach like somebody breathing in their sleep. Away from the moon the stars go down to the water. The heater gives up its last warm breath on their feet. She leaves the radio on, low, a slide guitar from the station out of Santa Barbara, coming and going.

She gets out, barefoot on the cold dirt, and comes back from the trunk with the striped Mexican blanket that still smells of surf wax and somebody’s dog. She doesn’t go around to her side. She opens his door and climbs in over him, blanket and all, and settles in his lap with it around the both of them like a tent. It takes some doing. Her elbow finds the window crank and his ear; the blanket gets caught on the door lock and has to be negotiated with; her cap comes down over her eyes and she leaves it there and kisses him blind, laughing, until he pushes it back up with one finger and finds her looking at him.

The Saab’s passenger seat was not built for this. His knee is jammed against the glovebox and her back is against the dash, and when she reaches down past his hip and finds the seat lever and pulls it, the seat drops back two notches with a crack like a starter’s pistol, and she laughs into his neck. “That’s the most exciting thing that’s ever happened to this car.” “I doubt that.” “You’d be amazed. It’s a very Lutheran car.”
She gets the Carhartt off him first, all the way this time, one sleeve and then the other, and pitches it over the seat into the back on top of *Rumours*.

body.text: “All the way off,” she says. “I put that in writing.”

body: The flannel comes off over her head in the cold, knocking her cap off with it, and she laughs again at the cold on her bare arms — there’s a thin gray camisole under it, and gooseflesh, and the moon on her shoulders. She does his shirt buttons from the bottom up, fast, and pushes it open, and puts both her hands in flat against his chest over his heart. They leave cold prints that warm. His hands go under the hem of the camisole to her bare back: the long muscles either side of her spine, the knobs of it, the cage of her ribs going in and out under his palms with her breathing. Her skin is hot where the blanket is and cold where it isn’t, and he can feel the line between.

body.text: His hands don’t stay where he kept them in the lot. She noticed that too, and says so, into his mouth, without words.

body: Her mouth goes to his collarbone. She finds the St. Michael there on its chain, warm from him, and lifts it off his chest with one finger and looks at it in the moonlight — the saint with his sword up and his foot on the devil — and lays it over his shoulder, down his back, out of the way.
“Excuse us,” she tells it.

Something in him flinches for the saint and is overruled. The medal lies cold against his spine under the blanket. Her thumb comes up and finds the scar through his eyebrow and runs along it, once, in the dark. “Still not buying Erie,” she says, and kisses it.

She kisses him with her hands in his open shirt and her bare foot braced on the dash, and the windshield fogs around her heel. It isn’t the harbor, fast and funny with a clock on it. It’s slower than that and hungrier, her teeth at his lower lip, his mouth at the side of her neck below her ear where her hair is still flat from the cap, her hips settling down onto him under the blanket, her other foot cold as a river stone against his shin where his jeans have ridden up. He learns her back with his hands, the warm hollow at the base of it, the two dimples there, the place between her shoulder blades where she shivers when he finds it and tells him not to stop finding it. There is no hiding anything in a Saab with her in his lap, and his body isn’t trying; she knows, and settles closer, and laughs, low, when his breath goes.
She stops long enough to say it, with her mouth an inch from his and her hand flat on his chest.

“I want this,” she says. “You. Here. More of it. I haven’t wanted anything this much since I was fifteen and wanted a part.” She takes one of his hands off her back and moves it around and puts it flat on her bare stomach under the camisole, and holds it there with her own. “That. I want that.”

On the radio the slide guitar has given way to a man in Santa Barbara with a voice like a bedroom, telling the Central Coast it’s two in the morning and he’s still here if they are. Down the coast the light comes around.

choices.text: Be the one who slows it.
choices.key: In a turnout where the coast turns, with the blanket around you both, you were the one who slowed it.
response: He slows it. His hands go still on her, his mouth slow at hers, and nothing else moves.

She laughs against his mouth. “You’re doing it again. The slow thing. It’s *infuriating*.” Then she takes it off him and uses it: she matches him, slower than he is, her mouth barely on his, her hips settling onto him under the blanket a quarter inch at a time, until slow is the worst thing that has ever happened to him and she can feel that it is and keeps doing it. “You started this,” she says, very quietly, and doesn’t stop.

choices.key: In a turnout where the coast turns, you let her lead.
response: He lets her lead, and she leads further. The camisole goes the way of the flannel, over her head and somewhere onto the floor of the Saab, and there is her skin and the moon on it and the gooseflesh coming up under his hands, and his mouth at the place where her collarbone ends, and her hands under his open shirt at the small of his back, pulling him up into her. The cold doesn’t seem to apply to her. Her heart is going hard enough that he can feel it in his own mouth.
She doesn’t stop, and he doesn’t, and down the coast the light comes around, and goes, and comes around.

choices.text: Tell her out loud what you want.
choices.key: In a turnout where the coast turns, you told her out loud what you want.
response: So he tells her. Her. This. That he thinks about it at the sink with his arms in the Hobart to the elbow, and on his father’s porch in his grandmother’s afghan, and at the 12:10 Mass, which he isn’t proud of. That he wanted it in the lot six days ago and on the plane and on the ramp at the harbor, and that he wants it now.
She takes his face in both her hands and looks at him in the moonlight, a long time, with the light coming around behind her down the coast. Then she kisses him once, hard, for saying it.
And then for a long time she doesn’t let him say anything else.

She sees his face. “That’s a bad face,” she says. “Is somebody dead?”

He finds her flannel on the floor under his boots and holds it out to her. “*Copriti*,” he says — what Nonna says to every Costigan going out her storm door. “Put a sweater on.” She laughs till the seat creaks, and pulls the flannel on over her head inside out, and doesn’t fix it.

body: She drives the coast back like a scene she’s waited her whole career to play: top down, radio off, both hands on the wheel at last, the Saab complaining on the grades in a voice he has never heard it use, her cap gone somewhere under the seat, her flannel inside out, dead sober and grinning at the road. She takes the cattle guard at forty and the ranch road’s dust goes up white behind them in the moon. On the highway she passes Duane, or somebody very like him, and gives him a two-tap on the horn. At the top of the grade she reaches over without looking and puts her cold hand flat inside his open shirt, over his heart, and leaves it there for a mile, driving one-handed, like she’s checking it’s still going.

On the long grade down, with the speedometer somewhere it shouldn’t be, she asks him how many candles now. On his wreath. “One. Two tomorrow. Sunday.” “So you’re halfway.” “A quarter.” “Don’t do math at me at three in the morning.” A truck; the two-tap. “What do you do with the waiting, in between? Just wait?” “Mostly. You’re supposed to stay awake.” “You’re doing great,” she says.

Somewhere past Ellery his back goes cold in one small place, and he reaches over his shoulder for the St. Michael where she put it, and brings it around on its chain, and settles it back where it goes. She sees him do it. “Is he mad at me?” “He’s seen worse.” “That’s not a no,” she says.
At the Marine Lab turnout she stops short of the chain with the engine running. He has the door open and one boot on the dirt when she says it, to the windshield.
“I don’t take people home.”
He looks back at her. “Why?”
“I’ve never wanted to yet.”
*Yet*, he hears. She leaves it in. It comes to him, with the door open and the cold coming in over the sill, that he doesn’t know where she sleeps when she’s up here.
“Go,” Skye says. “Your building’s on fire.”

s12.slug: SATURDAY · 3:38 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE LAWN
body: He hears it from the Lagoon path: the Delgado alarm, the same goose-honk it has made at three in the morning since August, coming to him across the black water a quarter mile out. She left him at the Marine Lab turnout at 3:33 with her flannel still inside out, and the one taillight was gone around the bend on Ocean Road before he’d gone ten steps. He runs. The path is dark under the eucalyptus and loud with his own boots, and the cold comes in through the open shirt. He buttons the shirt while he runs and gets it wrong by one hole, top to bottom.

He comes onto the lawn from the wrong side — up from the water, out of the eucalyptus, not out of the door — past Rafi Ochoa sitting on the curb of the path in a hooded surf poncho, who watches him come up out of the trees at a dead run and says, approvingly, “Boss.” And into the tail of Alarm Five: three hundred people in towels and comforters and somebody’s sleeping bag on the wet grass under the trees, the horn still going, a Marisol Fire engine idling on Anacapa Way with its lights turning over all of them because this is the fifth time, and the moon up over the lawn like it bought a ticket.

Priya is in the middle of it with the laminated roster on a clipboard and a headlamp on her forehead. On the back of the clipboard, facing the crowd, a second laminate: FIFTH TIME. I KNOW. Every name on four has a check by it but one. A firefighter in a turnout coat leans down to ask her if everybody’s out, and Priya tells him everybody but one, and that the one is being *accounted for*, in a voice that makes him straighten up and go back to the engine.

Theo stands in front of her in the navy silk robe with the gray camera bag and the black bag both on his shoulder, mid-sentence. “— a condition, very Catholic, they do it in silence, it’s a whole tradition, there are *orders* of it —” He sees Jack over her head, coming up out of the trees, and doesn’t miss a syllable. “And there he is. Out of the shower.”
Priya turns. The headlamp turns with her and gets him full in the face.
“Costigan.” She lowers the clipboard. “You were not on my lawn.” The headlamp goes down him and comes back up. “You’re *dry*.”

Lena is sitting on the grass beside Laney under Laney’s pink comforter, with the quilt off her own bed around her shoulders. She’s looking at the strip of empty grass beside Theo, about the width of a person. Then she looks at him, coming up from the water at 3:38 in last night’s clothes, with his shirt done up wrong and the moon on him. She has nothing to say about it.
Laney has plenty. “Fireman,” she says. “You’re *dressed*.”

Kevin is running the other half of the roll with his own clipboard, in the navy quarter-zip and plaid pajama pants. Beside COSTIGAN, in pencil, Jack can see from here, there’s a small neat question mark. Down at the far end of the building Doug Pruitt stands barefoot in the wet grass with his pillow under his arm, blinking at the fire engine.
His shirt is wrong from the collar down, and he can still feel exactly where her hand was under it.

s12a.slug: SATURDAY · 11:40 AM · THE MARINE LAB TURNOUT, OCEAN ROAD

body.text: its daylight. marine lab turnout. 1140. you can ask now

body: There’s a great deal of light at the Marine Lab turnout. He has only ever had the place by a sodium lamp or the moon, or not at all, a chain and a sign at the edge of somebody’s headlights; at twenty to twelve on a Saturday, with his hair still wet from the shower, it turns out to have colors. The chain across the service drive is rust and salt. The sign about the tide pools has a harbor seal painted on it, peeling. The ice plant runs down over the lip of the bluff red at the tips, and past it the Channel is lit all the way out to the islands, so bright he has to take it in pieces, and the gulls on the guardrail stand around in it with their eyes shut.

The Saab is nosed up to the chain with the top down, pinker in the sun than he knew and more dented, a crease down the rear quarter panel he could lay his forearm in and a dimple in the trunk lid the shape of somebody’s knee. A long black garment bag hangs zipped from the passenger headrest, for tonight, and so she isn’t in either seat. She’s sitting up on the back of the car where the top folds down, with her bare feet on the back seat and sunglasses on and her hair wound up in a knot with a yellow pencil stuck through it, and a booklet open on her knees.

He knew about the freckles. He didn’t know there were this many, or that they went on down her neck into the collar of her T-shirt. There’s a tiredness under her eyes from whatever sleep she got, wherever she got it, and the faint crease of a pillowcase still on one cheek. It’s the first time he has seen her in daylight.
She hears his boots on the gravel and takes the sunglasses off to look at him. She looks for a good while.

“I had a theory,” she says. “That it was the dark. Everybody looks better to everybody at two in the morning. It’s a known fact. My entire industry is built on it.” She folds the sunglasses and hooks them in the neck of the T-shirt. “It isn’t the dark.” She says it the way somebody reports good results from a test they were afraid of, and she doesn’t bother hiding that she’s pleased.

She leans down off the back of the car and puts her thumb on his cheekbone, just under the eye, and turns his face to the sun. “You have a freckle. There. I’ve kissed that in the dark about forty times and never seen it.” She lets go of his face. “I’m going to be insufferable about it.”
“You said I could ask.”

“I did say that.” She holds up the booklet. It has the university’s seal on the cover over PRACTICE PROBLEMS, and the corner has gone soft from her thumb, and every page he can see has been erased down to a shine in places. “It’s for the math placement test. They mailed it to me.”
“I’m starting in January,” Skye says. “Here. Spring. Undeclared.” She turns a page. “I’ve declared enough.”
Something gets to his face at *January* and *here*, and he feels it get there, and she sees it. She goes on anyway.
“In Montecito,” he says, “you said not yet.”
“It’s yet.”

He puts a boot up on the bumper, and she moves her feet to make room on the seat, and he sits on the side of the car below her with the booklet between his knee and hers. The page she’s on is fractions. Every problem on it has been tried at least twice.

“I haven’t done math since I was fourteen,” she says. “Not on purpose. On a set you get a studio teacher. It’s the law. Three hours a day, in a trailer, in between setups, twenty minutes at a time.” She pulls the pencil out of her knot, and her hair comes down around her shoulders, and she rubs out an answer with the eraser, hard, while she talks. “Mine was a woman named Irene who knitted socks for her grandchildren in Fresno. She taught me the Louisiana Purchase without dropping a stitch. Every time we got to fractions, somebody knocked on the trailer and said they needed me in five, and Irene would say *go on, honey*, and fractions lost to the light every time. After a while Irene stopped bringing them up.” She blows the eraser crumbs off the page into the back seat. “At sixteen I took a proficiency test, in a trailer in Valencia, on my lunch, so I could be done with school.” She considers the Channel. “I’d never been to one to be done with.”
“You’ve never been in a high school.”

“Not even to vote.” She turns the page back. “And the network’s sending Cassidy away to boarding school in the spring. She’s already *at* a boarding school, there’s a lake, it’s the premise. They’re sending her to a different one. In Switzerland. Off camera.” Her face is bright with it. “So we’re both going off to school. I think that’s the funniest thing that’s ever happened to me, and I’m the only person at the network who does.”
She’s working the eraser again, at a seven-twelfths that isn’t right, and she doesn’t look up from it.

“Sharks were a lie,” she says. “I’ve never been bad at anything where anybody could see my face. I was good at being eleven. I was good at crying on a dock. A few million people watched Cassidy cry on that dock, and I was fine, because I was good at it.” She rubs until the paper pills. “Twenty eighteen-year-olds in a room, watching me get seven-twelfths wrong.” She blows the crumbs off. “I’d take the shark.”
“Show me,” he says.

She hands him the booklet, and after a moment the pencil. He draws a circle in the margin and cuts it into twelve like a pie, the way he did it for Gina at the kitchen table on Glenwood for three winters running, with Nonna saying from the stove that in her day they had used actual pie. He doesn’t hurry it. A fraction is only a thing cut up fair, he tells her; the bottom number is how many pieces, the top is how many you’ve got, and once the knife’s gone in, the bottom number doesn’t change for anybody. He shades seven of the slices, and then three of them over again, and lets her look.

She sees it at once. It was never the math; he can watch it go into her like a key into a lock she’s had the whole time. She takes the pencil back off him and does the next one herself, and the one after, fast, in a hand that slants downhill.
She starts casting them.

“Five-twelfths,” she says to the page, flat, bored, a woman behind a folding table at the end of a long day. “Too tall. *Next.*” Her pencil moves. “Two-thirds. Love what you’re doing. We’re going a different direction.” She circles an answer. “Three-fourths. Thank you so much for coming in, we have your headshot.” She gets every one of them right, and winds her hair back up and runs the pencil through it, and the knot holds.
“You don’t make it a favor,” she says. “When you explain something. Everybody who’s ever explained anything to me did it like they were doing me a favor.”

There are stairs down the bluff below the sign, railroad ties sunk into the ice plant with sand on every tread. She goes down them ahead of him barefoot with the booklet rolled up in her back pocket, and goes out across the rocks at the bottom quick and flat-footed, without looking down, her arms out for balance she doesn’t need. The rocks are black and wet and pocked with pools, each with its own small business going on in it: turban snails, a crab the size of a thumbnail backing away into a crack, a scatter of green anemones folded shut. She crouches over the biggest pool and puts her finger straight into the middle of one, and it closes on her, slowly, all the way to the knuckle.
“It likes me.”
“It’s trying to eat you.”
“Same thing, where I work.”

The rock is cold under her feet and she doesn’t seem to notice it. The sun is all over her, her hair, the freckles, the hand in the pool. He steps across to the next rock to see the anemone better and the rock isn’t where his boot thought it was, and he goes into the pool beside it to the knee, and the Pacific comes in over the top of his boot like a bucket of ice. She laughs so hard the anemone lets go of her.

She kisses him there, with him standing in the pool and her on the rock above it, so that she has to bend down to do it. It’s short. Her mouth is warm and tastes of salt, and there’s salt on his own, and a gull on the next rock over watches all of it with one yellow eye like it paid to get in. She’s laughing at his jeans before it’s over.
He climbs out and sits on a dry rock and pours the Pacific out of his boot. She sits down beside him with her feet in the pool and her face up to the sun and her eyes closed.
“When I said January,” she says, with her eyes still shut, “you did a face.”
He opens his mouth.

“No, I know what it was.” She opens one eye at him. “It’s your church people. Your casserole people. The ones who are going to pray for me. *At* me. Holding hands.” She shuts the eye again. “Your church people are going to hate me.”
“It isn’t —”
“It’s fine. I’m very easy to hate in person. It’s a gift.” The sun is on her eyelids. She lifts her finger out of the water to look at it, and puts it back in to see if anything else will have her.

response: “I want you here,” he says.

She opens her eyes and turns her head to look at him in the sun without the glasses, the freckles and the tired and the salt drying white on her ankles. “In daylight,” she says. “You said that in daylight.”

response.text: “Here,” she says. “Where everybody you know is. Thursday you said you’re keeping me from all of them.” “I said I hadn’t worked it out.” “You’ve got till January.”
