s13.slug: SATURDAY · 2:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: The basement laundry room smells the way it always does on a Saturday afternoon, sweet and chemical, warm lint and somebody’s dryer sheets, and Jack comes down the stairs into it with a pillowcase full of everything that smells like surf wax and somebody’s dog.
Theo is sitting on a dryer.

Theo sends his laundry out to a woman in town who irons his T-shirts. He has never used a dryer in this building. He is sitting on top of Dryer 3, under Priya’s laminated sign about the quarters, in his loafers, with his ankles crossed. Laney is cross-legged on the folding table with a legal pad on her knee and her sunglasses on, indoors, in a basement. Their heads are together over the pad.
They come apart.
“We were discussing —” Laney says, “— finals.”
At the same moment, Theo: “The situation.”

Laney turns the legal pad over on her knee. On its cardboard back, in Sharpie: PROPERTY OF PI LAMBDA CHI — DO NOT REMOVE FROM HOUSE. On the dryer at Theo’s hip there’s a box of laundry soap with the price tag still on it.

They don’t leave. Jack takes the washer at the end of the row, and the two of them give their attention to the ceiling — the pipes, the sprinkler heads, a water stain over the door that Theo regards with real interest. Jack upends the pillowcase into the machine: the flannel, the jeans, the shirt he buttoned wrong.

“It’s a study group,” Theo offers. “For finals. We meet down here for the acoustics. Laney has a theory about the dryers — the white noise, the warmth, it’s very good for retention, they did a study at Stanford, or one of the Stanfords. Every Saturday. Two-thirty. Very exclusive.” He re-crosses his ankles. “You’d hate it.”
Laney doesn’t look at Theo while he says any of it. She’s watching the shirt go into the machine. “Jack,” she says. “Separate your darks.”

response: “Finals,” Jack says. “In the laundry room.”
Theo indicates the room — the dryers, the folding table, the sign about the quarters — with one open hand. “It’s a situation room.”
Laney nods at that, as if it settles it, and goes on looking at the pipes.
He picks the darks back out without a word and puts them in the next machine over, and feeds both of them quarters.
Laney leans over to Theo, low, not low enough. “He *separates*.”

choices.text: “If you want to know where I was, ask.”
response: “If you want to know where I was,” Jack says, “ask.”
Laney looks at him over the legal pad. “We don’t want to *know*, Jack. We want to *guess*.”
Theo says nothing at all.

s14.slug: SATURDAY · 3:35 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSION LINE
body: At half past three the sun is low enough to come in through the blue glass sideways, and it throws the windows across the side aisle in long blue panes, one to a pew. The confession line waits in them on folding chairs, under the ribs of the hull, six people facing the old coat closet and its card in Mrs. Fitch’s capitals: KNOCK (gently). Mrs. Fitch has the card table by the door, a tin of lemon bars, and her ears open.
Jack has the chair nearest the closet. Joey Abruzzo has the one behind him.
“*Jack!*” Joey leans forward to his ear at full Staten Island volume. “Big one?”
“*Joseph*,” says Mrs. Fitch, from the door, without looking up.
“Sorry, Mrs. Fitch,” Joey whispers, at the same volume.

A minute later he’s back at Jack’s ear. “You see Tiger’s statement? *Personal sins should not require press releases.*” He nods at the closet door, very pleased with it. “That’s this. This is the opposite of a press release.”
At the card table Mrs. Fitch fills in a word. “He’s not wrong,” she says, to the crossword.
The closet door opens, and a girl from the choir comes out with her face scrubbed and goes up the aisle to the votive rack. It’s his turn.

s14a.slug: SATURDAY · 3:50 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSIONAL
body: The coat closet is the size it has always been: a kneeler on this side, a folding chair on the other, and in the middle the linen screen on its wooden frame, with a shape behind it in a purple stole. The coat hooks are still on the back wall from 1962, and somebody has thumbtacked a holy card of the Prodigal Son to the inside of the door at eye level, where only the penitents see it. Jack kneels. On the far side of the linen the chair creaks, and the bad leg finds its place, and Osei settles and waits for him with all the time in the world.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned.”

body.text: “It’s been two and a half weeks since my last confession.” The last penance is done; he finished it at the first candle, in Youngstown.

body: He has the next part ready, and it still comes out in pieces. “There’s a girl,” he says. “Not the one I —” He stops. “A girl.”
The shape behind the linen waits.

“I keep putting myself where I know what’s going to happen,” Jack says. “In her car. Two in the morning. Up the coast somewhere, where nobody knows where I am.” His knees hurt already. “I don’t stop it. Monday it was her phone that stopped it — an alarm she set so she’d leave. Last night it was the fire alarm in my building, three miles off, by text. I didn’t set either one.” Outside the door, faintly, Joey Abruzzo is explaining something to somebody about the Yankees. “And then I go again.”

body.text: “Last night I was the one who slowed it down,” he says. “Slowed it. I don’t know if that counts.”
“Last night,” he says. “Further.”
“Last night I told her what I want,” he says. “Out loud. I meant it.”

body: “And the rest of the week.” He leaves it there, without a list, and Osei leaves it with him.
On the other side of the linen a long breath goes out.
“I was a doctor before I was this,” Osei says, “and a doctor asks the dull question first, because it is the one that tells him where it hurts. Do you want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens?”

response: “Stop what happens,” Jack says. “Not her.”

“Then change the hour.” Osei says it like a prescription, something to take with food. “The near occasion is rarely the person, my friend. It is two in the morning, and a car, and nobody who knows where you are. Bring her into the daylight.” A pause, and the chair. “If she won’t come into the daylight, that is also an answer.”

body: He gets up off the folding chair. Behind him Joey Abruzzo’s eyebrows go up.
“Go ahead, Joey.”
Joey goes ahead at speed, and Jack hears him knock anyway, gently, on the open door.
At the card table by the door Mrs. Fitch doesn’t look up from her crossword. “Not today, Mr. Costigan?”
“Not today.”

“Father’s here till a quarter to five,” she says, filling in a word. “And next Saturday. And the one after. He’s very reliable. It’s one of his only faults.” She takes the lid off the tin anyway and holds it out to him, the way she would to anybody, and he takes a lemon bar. Outside, the A-frame’s courtyard is bright enough to make him squint after the blue, and he has a shift at seven and four hours to fill before it. He sits on the steps with the lemon bar and watches the broken sprinkler in the courtyard work at the olive tree, a click at a time, missing it every time.

At ten to one on a Saturday night the Anchor smells of coffee that’s been on the burner since ten, bleach water, and pie. The Hobart is on the last rack of the shift. Rudy’s transistor, on the shelf over the grill, is playing a ranchera at a volume meant for Rudy, and the room is down to its dregs: two fishermen at the far end of the counter in white rubber boots, not talking, and in the corner booth a couple at the end of a date that went wrong somewhere around the soup, both of them reading the dessert card for the third time.
Gloria backs in through the swinging door with a bus tub of cups on her hip and sets it on his drainboard. “Your pecan’s at the counter, hon.”

Jack looks out through the pass. Lena is on the third stool from the register in the cardigan and her boots, her hair coming down out of a pencil, with Kevin Tran’s keys on the Formica in front of her — the Bellarmine lanyard and the Honda key. Beside the keys is a slice of pecan pie on a saucer with the fork laid across the top. It hasn’t been touched. On a stool by herself at ten to one, with the keys in front of her, she looks like somebody waiting for a bus that may not run this late.
He comes out drying his hands on the apron, and she gets there first. “I was in the neighborhood.”
“It’s three miles.”
“I have a minivan.” She lifts the keys off the counter and lets them swing. “I told Kevin it was an errand. He said, ‘Sixty-five, not sixty-six,’ and went back to his flashcards.”

She gives him the inventory at a clip. “Julian’s in Oakland. His brother’s home on leave — Daniel, he’s in the Navy, he’s got two weeks, and his mother is cooking for a regiment. He asked me to come up for it.” Her hand goes to her throat, to the medal, and turns it on its chain. “I have a paper. Laney’s at the Pi Lam Christmas semiformal in a dress that’s a felony in Texas, and she’s sleeping at the house. Margot went to bed at ten like a Lutheran. And I am eleven and oh, and I can’t sleep.”
“I’ve got a rack in,” Jack says. “Ten minutes.”
“I’ve got pie.” She looks at it. “Gloria chose it. I asked for the coconut, and she said coconut was for people who’d made up their minds.”

Back at the sink he runs the rack and pulls it out steaming. Gloria comes and stands at the pass with her order pad, not writing on it, and looks out at the counter. To Jack, low, without turning her head: “Pecan came to see if you were here.”
She goes out with the pot to the fishermen.
At eight minutes to one he comes out and sits on the stool beside Lena’s in his apron, and she picks up the fork and starts on the pie.

“Alabama beat Florida,” she tells him, with her mouth full. “Remy called me from Baton Rouge at nine o’clock screaming, and I honestly couldn’t tell you if it was joy. Tebow cried. On national television. I am not proud of how much I enjoyed it.”
“You’re eleven and oh. You can afford to be gracious.”
“I can afford pie,” Lena says. She tips her head at the corner booth without looking at it. “What did Gloria give them?”
“Two-crust,” Jack says. “Both of them.”
“Separately?”
“She says that’s the problem.”
The RAZR goes off in the apron pocket.

She takes the Odyssey up Mission at exactly the limit with Gloria’s cups in the cup holders, sitting forward over the wheel like the van might try something, and at the light by the bank Jack tells her what night it is.
“St. Nicholas Eve.”
“Lord. It is.”

He tells her about Glenwood Avenue. Rosie’s shoes are out by the front door tonight, both pairs, school and church, because she’s eight now and has worked out the arithmetic. And at St. Brigid’s, every year on the sixth, every kid in the school leaves one shoe outside the classroom door, and at six in the morning his mother lets herself in with her keys and fills them — two hundred shoes, an orange and a chocolate coin and a candy cane in each — and is back at her desk in the office with her coat off before the first bus pulls in. Twenty years.

“No.” She thinks about it through a green light. “He’s Greek.” And a block later: “Then we’re doing it.”
“We don’t have any shoes.”
“Delgado has four hundred pairs of shoes, Jack. They’re just inside the doors.” She signals for a lane change on an empty street. “People leave their shoes out. It’s what shoes are for.”

He thinks about the boxes while she drives: Florida oranges from the Giant Eagle in waxed cartons, the coins in a mesh sack from the wholesale place on Market Street, the candy canes that broke in their cellophane if you set the carton down wrong, and his mother going down the dark hall at St. Brigid’s with a list in her hand, checking names against shoes, saying them under her breath like she was taking attendance for God.

The Walgreens on Mission is lit like noon in an operating room, every tube in the drop ceiling going at once over the empty aisles, and out of the speakers in the ceiling tiles Darlene Love is begging somebody, at the top of her lungs, to come home. The cashier has on a tinsel headband and the face of a woman who has seen worse than two kids at twenty to two.

On the way in Lena stops at the rack by the register, where Tiger Woods is on the cover of three magazines at once, in three different shirts, with the same smile. She turns them around one at a time so they face the Tic Tacs. “He’s got two babies,” she says. “Someday they’re going to be able to read.”

Lena takes a basket and goes through the store like a raid. Every net bag of gold-foil coins off the Christmas endcap; two bags of clementines out of the case by the door; a box of candy canes. She stops under the speaker to read him the back of a coin bag. “‘Milk chocolate coins.’” She holds the bag up to the light. “They’re dowries, you know. He threw bags of gold through a man’s window at night so the man wouldn’t have to sell his daughters. Three girls, three bags. One went down the chimney and landed in a stocking somebody hung up to dry.”
“That’s where the stocking comes from.”
“That’s where *everything* comes from. Read your saints.”
The cashier has come out from behind the register to watch her clear the hook. “There’s another case in the back,” she says. “If you’re doing what I think you’re doing.”
Lena turns around with her arms full of gold. “Ma’am, you are an instrument of grace.”
“I’m an instrument of inventory,” the cashier says, and goes to get the case.
“How many coins in a shoe?” Lena says.
“Ma does one.”
“One.” She considers the bags in her arms. “Your mother is a Jansenist.”
“My mother is a school secretary with two hundred shoes and a budget.”
“Same thing,” Lena says, and puts two more bags in the basket.

In the candy aisle she stops, takes the pack of Reds out of the chest pocket of his Carhartt where the corner of it shows, shakes one out, and puts the pack back where she found it. “For the saint.” It goes into her cardigan pocket. “I’ll file it.”

She has been fast all night — the clip at the counter, the raid on the endcap, the dowries — and in the next aisle she slows down. It’s wrapping paper. She stops in front of it — a roll with reindeer, a roll with the Grinch — and reads the price on the reindeer, and she goes on reading it while she talks.

s17.music: Aaron Neville — “Tell It Like It Is”
body: The breakwater lot is a strip of crushed shell at the foot of the rocks with room for six cars, and at ten past two they have all six spaces. Lena leaves the engine running for the heater. The clementines ride between the seats in their orange nets, the coins in Walgreens bags at Jack’s feet, and out at the end of the rocks the harbor light blinks green on its pole — a light, not a lighthouse; it has never claimed to be anything else. On the bait dock the sea lions are having the argument they have every night.
Out of Kevin’s changer comes Aaron Neville, high and slow, on a CD Lena burned. “He keeps a slot for me,” she says. “It’s in his rules.”
Jack looks at the index card on the dash.
“The unwritten rules.”
The Loeb is on the dash too, small and green, with her pencil in it at Book Nine. Her Greek final is Tuesday.
“You’re studying,” Jack says.
“I’m *preparing*. Studying is for people who might fail.” She picks the Loeb up and opens it to the pencil and doesn’t look down at the page.
“Have you read it?”
“The Fitzgerald. Junior year. Mr. Pavlik made us do the Cyclops out loud in parts.”
“The Fitzgerald,” Lena says, the way she’d say *the Living Bible*. “All right. Who were you?”
“A sheep.”

“Of course you were.” She tucks one boot up under her on the seat. “*Outis*,” she says. “Nobody. That’s what Odysseus tells the Cyclops his name is. And when he puts the stake in his eye, and Polyphemus screams, and all the other Cyclopes come up the hill in the dark — *What’s wrong? Is somebody hurting you?* — he yells back out of the cave, *Nobody is killing me.* And they go home to bed.” She’s grinning. “Oldest joke in Western literature. And it’s a pun. They say, *Well, if nobody’s hurting you* — *mē tis* — and *mētis* is cunning. He’s Nobody and he’s Cleverness in the same word, and Homer lets him laugh about it in his heart.”

body.text: In his jacket the RAZR goes against the cup holder, a dry hum on the plastic, and then twice more, close together. He leaves it where it is, and knows exactly where it is.
Lena turns a page she isn’t reading. “Nobody’s very awake tonight.”

In his jacket the RAZR rings — the full ring, loud in the van over Aaron Neville. Jack finds the side key through the canvas and kills it without taking it out, without looking, like a light switch in his own house. “Nobody wants you,” Lena says, and turns a page. The message tone goes off three times while she looks for her line, and she finds it anyway.

body: “And then,” she says, “he’s out on the water. He’s safe. He’s made it. And he can’t stand it.” She sits up in the driver’s seat. “His men are begging him — *shut up, shut up, he’ll hear you* — and the Cyclops throws half a mountain at the sound of his voice and nearly swamps them, and he stands up in the boat and shouts it back at the island anyway. *If anybody asks who blinded you, tell them it was Odysseus. Son of Laertes. Of Ithaca.* His name, and his father’s, and his island. And it costs him everything, and he’s *right* to.” She taps the Loeb against the wheel. “A man who stays Nobody to get home gets home as nobody.”

“For his *name*, Jack,” Lena says, and holds his eye, and doesn’t take back a letter of it.

response: “The best line in Homer is a man getting away with a lie,” Jack says, “and you want him to apologize for it. *Nobody is killing me* is the best joke in three thousand years, and it only works if he keeps his mouth shut.”
She points the pencil at him. “That’s not a line. That’s a confession.”

She looks at him with the pencil still in her hand, not pointing it at anything. “Everybody,” she says. “Even the ones who say they don’t. *Especially* them.”

body: The CD goes on to the next song. Lena turns it down without looking and turns in the driver’s seat to face him, her back against the door and her boots up on the console, where Kevin’s rules have nothing to say about them.

“All right. Other way round,” she says. “There’s a man in a courtyard by a fire, warming his hands. And a girl comes up to him — a servant girl, nobody — and she doesn’t ask him his name. She asks him whose he is. *You were with him.* And he says, *I do not know the man.* Three times.” She closes the Loeb on her pencil. “And then the rooster. Luke has the best version — Luke always has the best version. The rooster crows, and the Lord turns around — he’s right there across the courtyard, they’ve got him tied — and he *looks* at Peter. That’s all he does. He looks at him. And Peter goes out and weeps bitterly.” “He stays nobody to get home. And they built the Church on him *after* he cried.”
“Peter didn’t have a boat to get away in,” Jack says.

“Peter had a *boat*, Jack. He was a *fisherman*. He had a boat all along.” She leans over and taps his knee with the pencil. “He went back to it, too. After. And that’s where he got asked.” She sits back. “But not yet. Right now he’s at the fire.”
“*Who do you say that I am?*” she says. “That’s the only question in the book. Everything else is footnotes.”
Her boots are on the console by his knee. The green light out on the rocks comes and goes on the side of her face, and she waits for him, the pencil going end over end in her fingers. It’s his turn.

choices.text: “Peter denied *Him*. Odysseus was only ever loyal to his own glory. You’re comparing a coward to a show-off.”
response: “Peter denied *Him*,” Jack says. “Odysseus was only ever loyal to his own glory. You’re comparing a coward to a show-off. One of them was scared and came back. The other one was never scared of anything but being forgotten.”

“I’m comparing two men who wanted to get home,” Lena says. “And only one of them got to stay. Odysseus gets back to Ithaca and Tiresias has already told him he has to leave again — walk inland with an oar on his shoulder till somebody asks him what it is. He wins and he still has to go be nobody somewhere.”
She puts the Odyssey in reverse and backs it off the shell and takes it up Mission toward campus, still arguing, with the Loeb open on his knee because she told him to hold her place.

choices.text: “Peter cried. Odysseus shouted his home address at a blind man.”
response: “Peter cried,” Jack says. “Odysseus shouted his home address at a blind man.”

Lena laughs and hits him in the arm with the Loeb. “He *did*. He gave him the *zip code*.” Then she points the Loeb at him. “And Peter told a servant girl he’d never heard of the man. You want to know which is worse?”
“Not really.”
“Me neither. That’s why it’s in all four Gospels.”
She puts the Odyssey in reverse and backs it off the shell and takes it up Mission toward campus, still arguing, with the Loeb open on his knee because she told him to hold her place.

choices.text: “And Peter got asked again. On a beach. Three times.”
response: “And Peter got asked again,” Jack says. “On a beach. Three times.”

Lena opens her mouth, and shuts it, and looks out at the green light at the end of the rocks. “…Damn it, Jack.” She shuts her eyes. “*Feed my sheep.* One for each time. I *hate* it when you use John.”
She puts the Odyssey in reverse and backs it off the shell and takes it up Mission toward campus, still arguing, with the Loeb open on his knee because she told him to hold her place.

choices.text: “You’d know about not asking. You’ve never asked your mother one question.”
response: “You’d know about not asking,” Jack says. “You’ve never asked your mother one question.”
It’s the winning move, and it wins. Lena takes her boots down off the console. She doesn’t answer him. She reaches over and turns the heater down a notch, and then another.
She backs the Odyssey off the shell and takes it up Mission toward campus without a word, and the Loeb stays shut on the dash.

s19.slug: SUNDAY · 2:40 AM · KEVIN’S ODYSSEY, MISSION STREET
body: Mission Street at twenty to three is a mile of dark storefronts — the bank, the shoe repair, the Greyhound depot with its one bench, the tattoo parlor with a neon heart switched off for the night — and the Odyssey goes up the middle of it at exactly the limit with nothing in front of it and nothing behind.

The light by the Walgreens is the long one on Mission, and it catches them. Behind its glass the store is still lit for surgery. The woman in the tinsel headband is facing the gum by the register, alone with Bing Crosby now.

body.text: She drives with both hands and her chin up and the heater still turned down, and the van gets cold around them a degree at a time. It has been three minutes of Mission Street without a word. At the light she says it quietly, to the windshield. “Penelope knew him by the bed.”

“Twenty years,” Lena says. “And he walks in the door in rags with a lie in his mouth, and she isn’t sure. Everybody else is sure — the dog’s sure, the old nurse is sure, his son’s sure — and she isn’t. So she tests him. She tells the maid, *Move the bed out of our room for him.* And he loses his temper, because it *can’t* be moved. He built it himself, around an olive tree that’s still growing up through the floor. The bedpost is the tree.”

She has both hands on the wheel and isn’t looking at him. “The two of them knew that. Them and one maid who kept the door, if you want to be Homer about it. That’s how she knew him.” The light is still red. “And then there’s the line. *They went gladly to the rite of their old bed.* Twenty years, and that’s what Homer gives them. One line.”
She stops there. The Walgreens hums behind its glass, and the light stays red, and she lets it.

choices.text: “Penelope waited twenty years for a man who lied his way home. That’s my point.”
choices.key: In Kevin’s Odyssey Lena gave you Homer. You said Penelope waited twenty years for a man who lied his way home.
response: “Penelope waited twenty years for a man who lied his way home,” Jack says. “That’s my point.”

response.text: “She didn’t wait for *him*,” Lena says. “She waited to be sure it was him. Those aren’t the same thing, and you know they aren’t.” The light goes green, and she goes, harder than Kevin’s card allows.
Lena doesn’t answer. The light goes green, and she goes.

choices.text: “Then he should have told her first.”
choices.key: In Kevin’s Odyssey Lena gave you Homer. You said he should have told her first.
response: “Then he should have told her first,” Jack says.

Lena looks over at him. “Yes,” she says. “He should have. He should have walked in the door and said, *It’s me. I built the bed.* He’d have saved everybody a book.” The light goes green, and she sits through some of it before she goes.

choices.text: “Some things you keep so everybody gets home.”
choices.key: In Kevin’s Odyssey Lena gave you Homer. You said some things you keep so everybody gets home.
response: “Some things you keep,” Jack says, “so everybody gets home.”
“Who’s everybody?” Lena says.
He doesn’t answer that. She doesn’t make him. She looks at him across the van as if he were a line of Greek with a word in it she can’t place.
The light goes green. She takes her foot off the brake and lets the question go with it.

choices.text: “What I said about your mother. That was me, not the argument.”
choices.key: In Kevin’s Odyssey you used her mother to win a point. At the light by the Walgreens you took it back.
response: “What I said about your mother,” Jack says. “That was me, not the argument.”
The light goes green, and she doesn’t go. “I know it was,” she says.

Mission Street is empty behind them back to the harbor. She sits through the green and most of the next red with her hands on the wheel, and reaches over without looking and turns the heater back up, one notch and then the other, and drives.

body: In the Anacapa lot she noses the Odyssey into Kevin’s space under the lamp and turns the key, and the heater ticks down into quiet, and the La Vang rosary on the mirror swings twice and stops. Behind them the back glass reads WHO DAT · 11–0 the wrong way round. The clementines sit between the seats. Across the lot Delgado still has a scatter of lit windows — somebody on three brushing his teeth with the blind up — going out one at a time. Lena puts the Loeb back on the dash where Kevin’s card can keep an eye on it.

body.text: She looks at him a long time in the dashboard light. “Okay,” she says. And then, reaching back between the seats for the bags: “We’re still doing the shoes.”

“We’re doing the shoes,” she says, flat. She gets out with the bags and stands by the van in the cold with her back to him and her breath going up white under the lamp, and she stays like that until he gets out too, and then she hands him the heavier bag without a word.

She turns the Loeb over in her lap and doesn’t open it. “Tell me sometime, then,” she says. It isn’t a question. It sounds like something going on a calendar. She reaches back between the seats for the bags.
She turns the Loeb over in her lap and doesn’t open it. “You said *sometime*,” she says. “I’m going to hold you to the word. It’s a real word.” She reaches back between the seats for the bags.
“You’d have made a terrible Greek,” Lena says.
“I’d have gotten everybody home.”
“You’d have gotten everybody home as *nobody*, Jack.” She says it without any heat, and then she reaches back between the seats for the bags.
She laughs at the windshield. “Odysseus would have hated you.”
“Odysseus would have *loved* me.”
“Yes,” she says. “That’s my complaint.” She gives him the Loeb to hold and reaches back between the seats for the bags.

journal.title: Duels with Lena
journal.text: Two–one after Labor Day; she paid her Sunday. Three–one after moral luck: mine; she said I argued it like it was mine. Now four–one. Friendship: mine, arguing both sides. She said she’d never forgive me. Wednesday she said she forgives me. I’d rather she hadn’t. Unofficial, the laundry room, midnight on her feast, no referee — the Little Way: Thérèse, on points. Unofficial, the Delgado kitchen, a Sunday, no referee — the rich young man: nobody won. She said: He looked at him and loved him. The roux came out perfect. Unofficial, the Brick, four in the morning, no referee — on the heart: nobody won. Official, Hale’s seminar, the day after the Anglicans — on leaving: mine. Five–one. Hale says I argued for leaving like a man who’s never been allowed to. Unofficial, Seacliff Road, Halloween, the hour that happened twice, no referee — on grace: hers. She wants to be asked. Official, Hale’s seminar, All Souls — whether the dead can be wronged: hers. Monica asked to be remembered at the altar, and she was. Five–two. Official, Hale’s table, the night after Fort Hood — go or come away: hers. Leave the light on, she said. Five–three. Unofficial, Kevin’s Odyssey, St. Nicholas Eve, no referee — Nobody: nobody. I said a thing about her mother to win it, and took it back at a red light.

body: At twenty past three the last lit window on the Lagoon side goes dark, and Lena says, “Now.” They go in by the side door with the Walgreens bags hugged to their chests so they won’t rustle, which they do anyway.

There’s a problem on every floor, and it’s laminated. Priya has posted it at both ends of every hall in her font: NO SHOES IN HALLWAYS (FIRE CODE). Delgado has obeyed. Door after door, and nothing outside any of them but carpet.
“Every door with no shoes gets a clementine and a coin,” Lena whispers on the second-floor landing. “He threw gold down a *chimney*. He’ll understand.”

Outside 217, Laney’s Uggs stand side by side on the mat in defiance of the fire code. “She airs them,” Lena whispers. “Like a vampire airs a coffin.” She fills the left one with clementines and the right one with coins until they won’t take any more, and lays a candy cane across the top of each.

body.text: Since the van she has handed him things without looking at him — the bag of coins, the box of candy canes, a clementine passed back over her shoulder. At the Uggs she has to look at him, to keep from laughing out loud in a hallway full of sleeping people, and that’s the end of it. It has lasted about five minutes.

body: Outside 204 Rafi’s flip-flops are lying where he kicked them, white with salt, in December. Lena fills them anyway. “The fire code doesn’t cover flip-flops,” she whispers. “Flip-flops are a state of mind.”

They work the hall door by door, Lena setting a clementine and a coin on every bare mat like she’s laying a table, Jack holding the bags open. On three there’s no mat at all outside 305. Lena sets a clementine on the carpet squarely in front of Margot’s door, studies it, and turns it so the stem faces the peephole.

On four, Doug’s Crocs are outside 420, green, toes to the wall. Lena fills them with real respect, and then she takes Kevin’s keys out of her cardigan, Bellarmine lanyard and all, and lays them on top of the coins in the left one. “Return to sender,” she whispers. “He’ll find them. Kevin finds everything.”

At 412 Jack holds up a hand — *wait* — and lets himself in. Theo is asleep with his face to the wall and one arm hanging off the bed, the Rolex still on it. Jack finds the good cordovan loafers on the closet floor by feel and carries them out, and sets them side by side outside 412, and fills them himself: two clementines, two coins, two candy canes crossed on top. Lena watches him do it from the hall with her arms full.
They run short on four. The last doors get a coin and no clementine, then a clementine and no coin, and Lena apologizes to each one under her breath.
At 401 she takes an index card out of her back pocket — she wrote it at the Walgreens register while Jack paid — and slides it into the frame of Priya’s door, under the laminated fire-exit map.

body.title: Index card, Room 401
body.text: ST. NICHOLAS OF MYRA — CHECKLIST: COMPLETE.

body: At five past four the doorknob of 401 turns.

They make the east stairwell with the door still swinging and flatten against the cinderblock on the landing. Through the wire glass Jack watches a headlamp come out of 401: Priya, in sweats, with a biochem text under her arm, on her way to the bathroom at the end of the hall. The beam crosses her own door, and stops, and comes back to it. Beside him Lena has both hands clamped over her own mouth. Her shoulders are going.
Priya reads the card by headlamp. “*Unbelievable*,” she says, to the hall. She pulls it out of the frame and takes it back into 401 with her, biochem and all. The bathroom, apparently, can wait.

On the landing Lena takes her hands off her mouth and folds over the rail and laughs into the crook of her elbow without a sound, until she can stand up straight. It’s ten past four. In the bottom of the last bag there are two clementines and two coins.

journal.title: Priya (RA)
journal.text: Laminates things. Owns an air horn. Her freshman roommate was Nora Calloway. The one rule she doesn’t laminate is for her. Three jobs: RA, the library overnight desk, orgo tutor. Failing orgo, she says. Her parents run a motel in Fremont and think she’s going to be a doctor. Re-laminated the laundry room at two in the morning, on her twenty-first birthday. Her mother’s text came in at the dryers. She didn’t answer it in front of me. Alarm Five: the only name on four she couldn’t check was mine. ‘Costigan. You were not on my lawn.’ Sunday at four in the morning she found a card on her door. ‘Unbelievable.’

s21.slug: SUNDAY · 4:30 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY ROOM
body: Somebody’s four a.m. load is turning in the end dryer — a towel and one sneaker, by the sound of it, the sneaker coming round every second turn and hitting the drum. It’s the only warm thing in the basement. The caged clock over the vending machines says half past four. The upright stands against the cinderblock with its fallboard down.

Lena is sitting on the folding table by the dryers with her boots hanging and the last Walgreens bag in her lap. Jack is standing, because if he sits down anywhere he’ll be asleep. She peels a clementine in one long spiral and hands him half of it without asking if he wants it.
“Rosie,” she says. “Are her shoes out right now?”
“Since after supper. Both pairs. Ma fills them before she goes up.”
“And what does Rosie think happens?”
“She thinks a Greek bishop comes in the mail slot.”
“Does he?”
“On Glenwood? He uses the side door,” Jack says. “It bangs.”
“Does your mama get one? Does somebody fill hers?”
“Pop does. An orange and a scratch-off from the Sunoco. Every year.”
Lena puts a hand on her heart. “That’s the most romantic thing I ever heard in my life.”
“She won four dollars once.”
“*Stop*.” She laughs. “Mémère wants to know if her candle worked. She asks every time Daddy calls.”
“Tell her Nonna’s home. Tell her she’s bossing everybody with one hand.”
“I told her. She wants it from you. In writing.”
“I’ll write her in Calabrese. She can get it translated.”

body.text: “You said she has my saint.” “She has it. Ma read her the back. She says you write in red like a schoolteacher.” “Like a *nun*,” Lena says. “Tell your mama like a nun.”

body: “Laney’s going to come home in last night’s dress and find an Ugg full of fruit,” Lena says, “and cry. She cries at the Folgers commercial. The one where the brother comes home.”
“Everybody cries at that one.”
“*You* don’t.”
“In Youngstown we cry at the Folgers commercial in the garage. With the radio up.”
“And you? What did you get in yours?”
“Same as everybody. One year Danny put a lump of coal in mine he got off the railroad tracks behind the Sheet & Tube lot. Ma made him go to confession.”
“For the *coal*?”
“For the tracks.”

Lena eats a section of clementine and considers the end dryer. She tells him what’s on the final — Book Nine at sight, and one essay she already has opinions about — and that the saddest thing in the book isn’t Odysseus at all. It’s Polyphemus, blind, the next morning, at the mouth of the cave, feeling the backs of his sheep as they go out, and talking to his ram. *Dear ram, why are you the last one out? You’re never last.*
“Odysseus is under it,” Jack says.
“Odysseus is *under* it. Holding on.” She points the half clementine at him. “Did St. Nicholas really punch Arius?”
“Slapped him. At Nicaea, in front of three hundred and eighteen bishops. They took his stole and threw him in a cell for it, and Our Lord and Our Lady came in the night and gave it back.”
“That’s apocryphal.”
“It’s in the icons.”

“*Everything’s* in the icons,” Lena says, delighted with him, and he’s delighted with her, and it goes on like that — whether a slap counts as a theological argument, whether Arius had it coming, whether you could get away with it at Hale’s table — until the last coin is out of its foil and she’s broken it in half and given him his half, and somewhere in the handing of it the laughing runs out.
She’s at his height on the table. He hadn’t noticed till it stopped being funny.

There’s chocolate on his thumb. She looks at it, and lets it be, and reaches up and turns his collar out where it’s been folded under since the stairwell, and squares it, and her hands stay there, on the Carhartt’s collar, her knees against the front of his jacket. Up close there’s clementine on her breath and a fleck of gold foil at the corner of her mouth, and the freckle at the hinge of her jaw that he has been not looking at since August. He wants her. He holds still and wants her, an inch from her face, while the sneaker comes round in the dryer and hits the drum. Her thumbs are on his collarbones through his shirt. She doesn’t move them and he doesn’t move, and the not-moving costs him everything he has left at twenty to five in the morning, and he pays it.

body.text: In his jacket, against her knee, the RAZR buzzes. Twice, hard, a pause, and again. He doesn’t reach for it. Her hands stop on his collar.

In his jacket, against her knee, the RAZR goes off — the message tone, three bright notes, loud off the concrete and the cinderblock in the empty basement. He doesn’t reach for it. Her hands stop on his collar.
Nothing happens. The phone has been off in his pocket since one o’clock, and the basement is quiet except for the dryer.

body: Lena steps back first. She lets go of his collar and swings her boots over and gets down off the far side of the folding table, so that the table is in front of her, and sets the Walgreens bag on it with the last clementine inside.

body.text: “You should get that,” she says.
“You should get that,” she says, and it’s colder than anything she’s said to him all night.

body: The dryer comes round. She looks at him across the table under the long tube light.
“Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something, Jack. You know I won’t.”

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Jack is on his bed in yesterday’s clothes with the blanket pulled up over them, where he has been since he came up from the basement at ten past five. He hasn’t slept. The Walgreens coins were the cheap kind, and the chocolate is still on his thumb.

body.text: At 5:12, under the blanket, he opened it. *1 New Picture Msg*, SKYE (MISFIT), 4:40 AM. The bar crawled across, and the picture came up the size of a stamp, and the screen was the only light there was.
*Picture Msg* · you work saturdays. this was saturday
*Picture Msg* · best no i ever got. heres what it cost you
*Picture Msg* · asking again

A hotel bathroom: a mirror the width of the wall, a marble counter, two gold taps curved like the necks of swans. This time she’s facing the glass. Her hair was put up for the party and is coming down on one side. The dress is something dark and close that shines where the light hits it, and she has unzipped it and pushed it down to her waist, where it has caught on her hips and is holding. Above it there’s a black strapless bra and the rest of her: her shoulders, her collarbones, the shadow of her ribs, her stomach, bare and warm against all that cold marble. One hand rests flat on her own stomach just above the dress, as if she’s thinking about pushing it further. Low at her hip, in the other hand, the white iPhone, taking it. Her face isn’t playing this time. She’s looking straight out of the mirror at whoever is holding the phone.

It hit him low and hard, under the blanket, in his clothes. The time on it was 4:40, and at 4:40 he was in the laundry room with Lena on the folding table at his own height and the end dryer turning, and this was what went off in his jacket against her knee. He shut it.
The RAZR is off, the way it has been since the Anchor. At some point after five he took it out, and he has it on his chest now, shut, under his hand. He hasn’t turned it on.

body: At half past five, with his eyes closed, he heard Theo get up in the dark and dress without the lamp, and open the door to the hall, and stop in it. The hall light came across the carpet to the foot of Jack’s bed. Theo didn’t move for the length of a Hail Mary and most of another. Then he went, barefoot. Jack would have heard shoes.

At twenty to seven he comes back. His khakis are wet to the shin, and above the wet there’s sand, drying pale in the creases. He has a gas-station coffee in one hand and, hooked on the fingers of the other, the spare loafers that were outside the door. He tips one over his desk, and a clementine rolls out under Rosie’s two princes and stops against the lamp. It has been wherever he’s been.
He turns around with the coffee. His eyes go to the RAZR shut on Jack’s chest under Jack’s hand, and rest on it, and come up.
“You look like you’ve been somewhere, Costigan.”
“So do you.”

Down the hall a shower starts. Theo drinks his coffee standing up. In the frame of his mirror Nonna’s twenty is still folded the way she folded it. Sand comes off his cuffs onto the carpet, a little at a time, and Jack watches it come and says nothing about it, and Theo watches the clementine.
“There was fruit in my shoe,” Theo says.
“St. Nicholas.”
“I’m Episcopalian. Lapsed.”
“He doesn’t check.”
“Pop says you’re coming for Christmas,” Jack says. “He said to tell you it isn’t a question.”
Theo sets the coffee down by the clementine. “I have things,” he says. “In LA.” A pause, long enough for the shower down the hall to change pitch. “Tell your father I heard him.”
He lies down on his bed in the wet khakis, on top of the covers, with his sandy feet off the end, and puts his arm across his eyes.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: wet to the shin, with a clementine out of his own shoe. ‘You look like you’ve been somewhere.’ So does he. Pop says he’s coming for Christmas. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’

journal.text: Came in barefoot at 5:20, sand and wet jeans. ‘Couldn’t sleep.’ There was a girl in our room. Sunday, Sept. 20, 6:10, wet to the shins and hay on his sweater: he says he runs now. Four miles. Barefoot. Sunday, Oct. 11, before light: wet to the shins again. He drives to where he runs. Sunday, Oct. 25, before light, at a motel above Lucia: up the path from the water, wet to the shin, sand on the cashmere. ‘Couldn’t sleep. Went to look at the ocean.’ Sunday, Nov. 1, Halloween’s morning after: asleep on his covers in the dinner jacket at seven, shoes on, sand to the knees, the hems wet. Sunday, Dec. 6, St. Nicholas: at half past five I heard him stand in the open door a long time, and go barefoot. Back at 6:40, wet to the shin and sand above it, with a gas-station coffee and the spare loafers in his hand, and the clementine I put in one of them.

A hotel bathroom: a mirror the width of the wall, a marble counter, two gold taps curved like the necks of swans. This time she’s facing the glass. Her hair was put up for the party and is coming down on one side. The dress is something dark and close that shines where the light hits it, and she has unzipped it and pushed it down to her waist, where it has caught on her hips and is holding. Above it there’s a black strapless bra and the rest of her: her shoulders, her collarbones, the shadow of her ribs, her stomach, bare and warm against all that cold marble. One hand rests flat on her own stomach just above the dress, as if she’s thinking about pushing it further. Low at her hip, in the other hand, the white iPhone, taking it. Her face isn’t playing this time. She’s looking straight out of the mirror at whoever is holding the phone.

It lands in him low, in broad daylight, with the lounge smelling of somebody’s toast. It was sent at 4:40, while this phone was off in his pocket in the basement and Lena was on the folding table at his own height, and it has waited for him.
The rest of her night he read under the blanket at five: a woman who asked her to bless a baby, a voice, the Pope, *ohio*, a piano in a pool.
And at 2:15, a minute after he killed her call:
you declined me. bold
Last in the heap, from two floors down:

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying.

journal.title: The whiteboard
journal.text: Margot’s, by annexation: USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD. Sully’s made the board: liturgical football, idolatry, my outfit. Margot wasn’t even there when I read it. She didn’t need to be. Now the chastity talk is up there too: both of us, voluntarily. Kenzie Rourke got her own line. Margot thinks she might not be an idiot. Category pending. C 6, B 5. The morning after the wake, under the total: TUESDAY — NO SCORE. (BEREAVEMENT.) October 9th, top of the board: LEIF ERIKSON DAY (OBSERVED). Columbus: see attached. Then: FERRER TOWER · THU 5:00 A.M. · “WHEN THE SAINTS GO MARCHING IN.” Suspects: a Catholic; a different Catholic. Laney added the Holy Ghost. Margot wrote it up for the Tide and didn’t name anybody. Halloween: AMERICAN GOTHIC (UNPLANNED). Both. C 7, B 6. Somebody drew a pitchfork. Sunday after St. Nicholas: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS — FLOORS 2–4. SUSPECTS: (THE CATHOLICS). Laney’s TIGER column has given up counting. It says MORE.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Doesn’t go here. Not yet, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for forty minutes, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. I told her about St. Nicholas.

body: He puts the phone in his pocket. Not on the arm of the couch, not anywhere a hand could pick it up: the front pocket of his jeans, with his own hand on it until it’s in.

Doug comes along the counter and holds out a second clementine, already peeled. Jack takes it. Doug goes back to the whiteboard. Jack eats it a segment at a time at the window, and it’s cold from the hall and sweet to the middle.

Down in the Anacapa lot Kevin’s Odyssey sits in the sun with WHO DAT · 11–0 on its back glass. The Saints are at Washington at ten, and the glass will want changing by tonight, one way or the other. Two floors down and along, the light is on in Lena’s window.
